I desire to take the earliest opportunity on going into Committee of Supply to consider the estimates for the Department of Labour, to bring to the attention of the Minister of Labour a matter of grave importance affecting labour conditions in the province of Nova Scotia. I refer to the strike at Springhill, where seme 1,600 employees of the Cumberland Railway and Coal Company have been on strike since the 10th of August, 1909, or just 18 months to-day. The Minister of Labour has been informed of the situation in Nova Scotia by letter and telegram, and in the ' Labour Gazette ' for a long period, and the situation is more or less familiar to him. I may say that I have not before this brought the matter to the attention of the House for the reason that since the passing of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act the Department of Labour has always taken the attitude that where that Act has been invoked and its machinery has been applied in a given case, that the action of the department would end there, and that if it were understood by those who invoke its machinery, that a resort could he had to the Department of Labour after the Act had been invoked, that it would tend to weaken rather than strengthen the machinery of the Act, and that therefore the parties to the dispute must, after the Act has been applied, resort to the arbitrament of war, and that the fittest must survive. I have kept in touch with the matter myself, and I find that at the very inception of this strike, or on the day before the men went out on strike, the Acting Deputy Minister of Labour wrote to the president of the United Mine Workers of America a letter, which I propose to read in full. It is fairly long, but it gives, in the shortest possible way, I think, the attitude of the department affecting questions of 'this character. It reads:



Ottawa, August 9, 1909.
Sir,-I have the honour to acknowledge your communication of August 3 in reply to the letter of the Deputy Minister of Labour of July the 28th in respect to the strike in the collieries at Inverness, N.S. Your communication has been referred to the hon. the Minister of Labour and the minister directs me to say that he has had under consideration that part of your letter in which you stated you are inclined to the opinion that ' if the-Department of Labour would investigate the situation in Nova Scotia they could do much to bring about a settlement of the difficulty in that province,' and has noted that in concluding your letter you express the hope ' that the Department of Labour may lend its influence to bring about a satisfactory settlement of the difficulties in Nova Scotia.'
With regard to the request that the department should investigate the situation or lend its influence to bring about a settlement the minister directs me to point out that the dispute at Glace Bay between certain of the employees of the Dominion Coal Company, members of a local union of the United Mine Workers of America and the said company, has already been the subject of government intervention by reference under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, and the report of the board appointed has been given to the public in accordance with the provisions of the Act. Were parties to industrial disputes encouraged to look indefinitely to government intervention or given reason to believe that the findings of boards appointed expressly for the purpose of inquiring into existing troubles, would be subject to further revision by the minister or other officers of the Department of Labour, it would seriously prejudice the effectiveness of the work of boards appointed under the Act and the value of their findings, and might only serve, having regard to industrial disputes generally, to prolong, rather than to minimize, the period of industrial strike.
Whilst the policy of the department in the matter of disputes referable under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act is as set forth herein, the minister wishes me to say that he will be pleased to discuss at any time with either of the parties to a dispute any of the facts or circumstances having a bearing upon the situation and best methods of effecting a satisfactory adjustment of existing differences.
I have the honour to be, sir,
Your obedient servant,
(Sgd.) GEEALD H. BROWN,
Acting Deputy Minister.
T. L. Lewis, Esq.,
President United Mine Workers of America, Indianapolis, Ind.
In that letter the attitude of the Department of Labour was very clearly defined, and there is something to be said in favour of it so far -as ordinary strikes are concerned ; but the strike at Springhill is an extraordinary one. As evidence of that, I have only to refer the hon. minister to the report of his deputy minister on industrial conditions in the coal fields of Nova Scotia. At page 31 of that report he Mr. RHODES.
will find the following remarks in reference to the strike at Springhill :
I found evidence of strong feeling as between the management and the employees of this company. Leading spirits among the men manifest much feeling, not to say bitterness, toward the management, not only toward the person of the general manager, but to all subordinate officials; and since all these were drawn, with4 one exception from the ranks of the men themselves, the presumption i-s at least favourable_ to the theory that any estrangement that exists is not due to one side alone. With such an influence as this dominant among the men it would seem to be impossible for any manager or official to bring about a condition of good relations.
At page 32 of the same report he will find the following :
One is forced, therefore, to the conclusion that there can be no speedy termination to the present struggle, and that it will be a. long-drawn-out contest unless some factor not now in evidence comes into play.
The record of strikes at Springhill, with which the minister is familiar, will bear out that expression. I believe that some five boards have sat under the Conciliation Act without alleviating conditions there, and there have -been some 23 strikes in a period of 22 years. So that the conditions at Springhill are abnormal. I need not point out that the town of Springhill is an unusually good mining town. There is a good class of men there. The very appearance of the town is pleasing to the eye, vastly different from that -of an ordinary mining town. Nor, need I take up the time of the committee to point out the disastrous results of this strike. In the country around the town of Springhill, and in fact throughout the whole county, the blight of this strike is felt. The revenues of the province have suffered from it to the extent of some thousands of dollars. I have shown you the -attitude of the minister and the department with reference to the strike at Springhill. But in July of last year there occurred a strike among the employees of the Grand Trunk railway. On July 19, the editor of the ' Gazette ' at Barrie, Out., sent the following telegram to the minister :
Strike of trainmen declared here last night 9.30. Passenger trains being run this morning undermanned by inexperienced men in train service, and public seriously alarmed. Can you do anything P
To which the minister replied as follows :
Your wire received and contents duly noted. Am preperad to lend good offices of government to fullest extent possible towards adjustment of present differences, and have so informed parties.
Then, in a letter addressed by the Minister of Labour to Charles M. Hays, presi-

dent of the Grand Trunk railway system at Montreal, he makes an effort to bring the parties together. In conclusion, he suggests that a way be found for arbitration, and adds :
If such a reference to arbitration, is agreed upon, all the necessary expenses incidental thereto will be met by the government.
Then, I find among other telegrams the following, which is typical, from the Minister of Labour to Wm. C. MacLaren, president of the Board of Trade of Brockville, Ont., under date of Montreal, July 29, 1910 :
Your telegraph July '29 received. The government is putting forth every effort to bring about a speedy termination of Grand Trunk dispute.
I could read a number of telegrams of the same tenor, but that may be regraded as typical. Then, at the conclusion of the strike I find that the Minister of Labour refers to his efforts in connection with the strike in the following terms, in a letter addressed to A. J. Anderson, Esq., Joint Secretary O. R. C. and B. R. T., Brockville, Ont. :
I much hope that the part taken by the Department of Labour and the government in helping to bring about a settlement of the differences between the members of the brotherhood whom you represent and the Grand Trunk railway will have commended themselves favourably to the members of the Brockville lodges.
So that the minister himself is not indisposed to take some credit for the settlement of that strike, and as to that I am not disposed to quarrel with him, I would be one of the first to congratulate him on settling a strike or upon doing anything he could to settle a strike, and I hope he will not withhold his efforts to settle the strike at Springhill.
If any proof were needed that the government did promptly intervene in this Grand Trunk Railway strike after the conciliatory board had sat on it, I could refer to the Toronto ' Globe * of Wednesday, August 3, 1910, in which I find this heading:
Grand Trunk Railway strike is over; an agreement is reached. The good work of Hon. M. L. Mackenzie King and Sir Frederick Borden.
Then the details are given. In this article, Mr. Garretson, a representative of the men, is quoted:
Further, said Mr. Garretson, I would like to pay my tribute to Hon. Mackenzie King and Sir Frederick Borden for their work in settling this trouble. They both did everything possible to reconcile the conflicting parties, and they are entitled to the thanks of not only the railroad interests, but of the people of the Dominion. By the manner in which they aided the negotiations they have earned I 107i
the gratitude of the railway and of the men and also of the whole public.
And the ' Globe ' not only refers to the matter in its news column, but also in its editorial column, from which I shall quote a few lines out of many:
The services, the very great servics, rendered by the Minister of Labour throughout this controversy have been of the highest value. Hon. Mackenzie King has illustrated what may be done by government representative with adequate knowledge, a sense of justice, a conciliatory spirit and an eye single to the good of the public.
The Montreal ' Herald ' is no less forward in giving its mede of praise to the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Militia, but I shall not take up time by quoting the article. I may refer briefly, however, to the government organ, the Ottawa f Free Press,' in its issue of August 3, 1910. It is just as fulsome in its praise of the two ministers I have mentioned. It says:
The usefulness of the Labour Branch of the Dominion administration has been doubly vindicated as the result of the recent dispute between the railway companies and certain of their employees. When, months ago, the companies were unable to come to terms with their men, a strike was made impossible because of the necessity under the Lemieux Act of first appointing a board of conciliation to investigate the dispute. The report of that board immediately solved the trouble so far as the Canadian Pacific railway was concerned, and an agreement which was mutually satisfactory was signed between the employers and the employed.
That was vindication number one. Unfortunately, that report did not, offhand, settle the dispute between the Grand Trunk railway and its men and open war resulted.
There was no law on the statute-book empowering the government to interfere. There was nothing to compel the disputants to submit to arbitration. So far as legislation was concerned, the government had no standing.
But while the government had no compulsory powers, it did have in the Labour Department machinery which it could at once set in motion with the object of bringing the regrettable war to an end.
Before the Labour Department was created, it was anybody's duty when a strike occurred to make an attempt to stop it, and what is anybody's duty is often nobody's duty. But things have changed. Immediately the strike occurred on the Grand Trunk, the eyes of the public were focussed on the Labour Department. Everybody said it was the duty of the Labour Department to act as mediator. There was no casting around for a man or men who would be unprejudiced with the delay consequent upon such a search, The one man at whom all pointed for this arduous and urgent task was the Minister of Labour.
Hon. Mr. King rose to the occasion and once more he has come out of the ordeal with flying colours.
The editorial goes on somewhat further, but I shall not quote any more. I have no

quarrel to find with the minister or the department for having intervened in the Grand Trunk Railway strike. All credit to them for having done so. As a matter of fact, if the Labour Department is to serve a useful purpose the Minister of Labour must exercise just such powers at Spring-hill as he did in connection with the Grand Trunk Railway strike. But if the Department of Labour is to content itself with merely sitting still and allowing the machinery to be invoked, and then, if the parties fail to come to terms under the Act, let them fight it out as in the old days before there was an Act, we might, just as well do away with the Labour, Department altogether, because otherwise all that would remain for the department to do would be to gather a certain amount of statistics, as was done before. In the strike which occurred in the town of Springhill, the department took the stand that it would not intervene after the machinery of the Lemieux Act had been invuked. But that is not apparently always the policy of the minister and the government, because we find that when there was a strike among the employees of the Grand Trunk railway, the minister did intervene. He might say that the policy of the department had changed since the strike at Springhill, but I would point out that the strike still exists there, and is still of great importance, and I hope my hon. friend will take the committee into his confidence and let us know why he has made this distinction between the two.

Lest my silence be misconstrued, I wish to say that I do not subscribe to the doctrine of the ' Free Press ' or the ' Globe '; but aside from that altogether, let me point out that having been intimately connected with the men who are affected by the Grand Trunk Railway strike-not speaking of the strike from second hand but from first knowledge-I say very emphatically, much as I regret it, that I cannot endorse the enconiums which have been showered by the press pn the minister or admit that the *settlement of the Grand Trunk Railway strike was a satisfactory one. The contrary position is the one I am forced to take. From my knowledge of the situation in the town of Allandale, a portion of the town of Barrie, and from my general knowledge of the matter, I know that the settlement does not absolutely remove all disputes, because I understand there are employees, who by reason of that settlement, are cut off from their pensions. There are numerous instances among the strikers in which men, who had been from 10 to 25 years in the service of the Grand Trunk railway, find that the company entirely repudiate any obligation in any way or to recognize as entitled to his Mr. RHODES.
pension any one who had been out on strike and was afterwards restored to the service. What the company say is that these men come back as new men. If I understood the minister correctly, these men would probably not get a pension. He cannot say whether the agreement does or does not cover cases such as those I Tefer to. I am not now saying that I condemn the minister nor that I applaud him, but what I say is that from my knowledge of the matter, the indications are that this settlement will be exceedingly unsatisfactory, and in all probability a very unfortunate one for the men. I understand the hon. member for Cumberland to be dealing with another matter, and, incidentally for illustration I presume, he finds it proper to refer to the Grand Trunk employees' strike. If I could add compliments to the Minister of Labour in relation to the Grand Trunk strike, I should be prepared to do so, and I may be able to do so in the end. At present I am not in that position. If I am to judge of the facts as they are before me, my reference to the matter must be uncomplimentary. For the present, however, I leave it. 1 am collecting information on the subject, and when I have collected it,
I may bring the matter again to the attention of the House.

I am sorry that my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) did not understand my object in referring to the Grand Trunk strike. My hon. friend the Minister of Labour did. I did not refer to it for the purpose of dealing with it. I pointed out that there has been a strike in my county for the last eighteen months. The policy of the department, i't was stated, was not to interfere with the strike where the machinery of the Act had been put in operation and had proved of no avail. But, in the strike of the Grand Trunk employees, the machinery of the Act was applied without effect, and yet after that the minister took it in hand. I was asking him the reason for this difference of treatment.

I think I understood the hon. gentleman (Mr. Rhodes) and said so.
I thought he was referring to the Grand Trunk strike incidentally and by way of illustration, while dealing with the case in his own riding with the facts of which he is specially familiar.

Replying, first, to my hon. [DOT] friend from Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes), I would say frankly that I agree with him that, to appearances there seems to be a difference in the action on the part of the department in regard to these two strikes. But I think he will agree with me that circumstances must govern actions at all times, and there are occasions when the

exception itself proves the rule. In regard to the general policy of the department as to intervening in industrial disputes, it is precisely as set out in the letter of August 9, 1909, written to Mr. Lewis by Mr. Brown, the Acting Deputy Minister of Labour. In that letter it is pointed out that where a dispute has come under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act it is not the policy of the department to follow up any intervention of that description by intervention on the part of any officer of the government or department. But my hon. friend will notice-for he has read it-that this communication closes with these words:
Whilst the policy of the department in the matter of disputes referable under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act is as set forth herein, the minister wishes me *to say that he will be pleased to discuss at any time with either of the parties to a dispute any of the facts or circumstances having a bearing upon the situation and best methods of effecting a -satisfactory adj ust-ment of existing differences.
In the ease of the Springhill strike, notwithstanding that this intimation was made some sixteen months ago, up to the present time neither of the parties to that dispute, so far as I am aware, has cared to take advantage of it. They have not intimated to me, either directly or indirectly, their desire to discuss the situation at Springhill with a view to bringing about a termination of the strike. The Grand Trunk strike was different. When it had assumed such proportions that there was hardly an interest in the province of Ontario that was not suffering in consequence of it, I received the following telegram from one of the representatives of the employees on strike at that time:
Montreal, Que., July 27, 1910. Hon. W. L. .Mackenzie King,
Minister of Labour, Ottawa.
Messrs. Garretson and Lee held a conference to-day with Mr. Hays without result. May I be permitted on behalf of the men on strike to request that, as a Minister of the Crown and representative of the people yon come to Montreal and by further effort try to arrange an honourable settlement either by arbitration or negotiation.

Mr. Murdock was a representative of the men out on strike at that time.
I point out to my hon. friend that there, at any rate, is a difference: in the one case the department has not been requested, up to the present time, to intervene further than by the action under the Act; in the case of the Grand Trunk strike the department was requested by one of the parties to the dispute to take action. I am sure my hon. friend will agree with me that, in the absence of any request from the parties after the communication that was sent them, it would hardlv have been proper for the department to have proceeded.
I say frankly that if the parties had come and discussed this matter with me I should have been only too glad, if a suitable way could have been found to have assisted to the extent of my power. I do not say that I would have intervened actively, but I would have endeavoured to assist in bringing about a readjustment. I may say that, without making it publicly known, I have had a talk with the present manager of the Springhill mines with a view to understanding the situation thoroughly, to see if, in some way, it would not be possible for the difficulty there to be brought to a close.
The hon. gentleman is referring to the new manager?

sumption is at least favourable to the theory thal any estrangement that exists is not due to one side alone. With such an influence as this dominant among the men it would seem to he impossible for any manager or official to bring about a condition of good relations.
That passage my hon. friend read, but on the next page, 32, we find:
One is forced, therefore, to the conclusion that there can be no speedy termination to the present struggle and that it will be a long drawn out contest unless some factor not now in evidence comes into play.
I read that also.

I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon; I did not catch that. In addition to the work which the Board of Conciliation did at Springhill, an officer of the department, the deputy minister, investigated the situation, went into it carefully and fully, and gave what he believed to be an honest and unbiassed report, so that both parties, if they chose, could be guided by it. Mr. Acland's report was made in September, 1909. He said to the parties that the strike would be a long drawn out fight. It was a question of recognition. He had heen in the confidence of the men on the one side and of the company on the other, and, speaking fearlessly as an officer of the department, he gave due notice to all parties concerned, that the strike would be a long struggle. 'That was in September, 1909. Here we are in February, 1911, and this struggle is still on. I say as a minister, speaking here, that I believe if the present position is maintained by the parties, in other words, if they insist on the Question of recognition, if we are here this time next year, this strike will still be in continuance at Springhill. I say that because I have had a conversation with the present manager, who has informed me that on no consideration whatever will his company yield on the question of recognition. If that is a fact, what can save the situation? There is no good of the department trying to intervene and bring about a settlement by negotiation. The only thing is for the parties to settle it themselves, and take such responsibility as the facts seem to warrant.
So I say in regard to the Springhill strike there was additional intervention on the part of the government disclosing the full nature of the dispute, disclosing, also, the only line on which a settlement could take place, but there was no special invitation as in the case of the Grand Trunk strike for any officer of the government to intervene.	_
But my hon. friend will also see that the strikes were very different in their significance. The Springhill strike has gone on for a year and a half, and conditions have continued in Nova Scotia pretty much as they have been for some years past. Un-Mr. KING.
doubtedly the locality immediately surrounding has been seriously affected, but the conditions generally in the province have not been. In the case of the Grand Trunk strike there was hardly a town in Ontario which was not beipg affected, in fact, some towns situated along the line of the Grand Trunk railway were really in the nature of communities in a state of siege. It was impossible to ship provisions in or manufactured goods out. Factories were closing, men were being thrown out of employment; the whole situation was one which was creating terror in the minds of the people of this province. A great system had been tied up from Chicago to Portland, a thousand miles of railway had been completely tied up, so far as the handling of freight was concerned. Boards of trade all over the province, city and town councils were sending telegrams daily to the government, and giving in detail the nature of the situation as it had grown up. There was a situation entirely different from a national point of view from the situation in Springhill. Had it been, as at Springhiil, local in its nature, I would have maintained the attitude that has been maintained in the case of the Springhill strike and have hesitated about intervening. But when we had a situation such as there was at that time, I felt that njo matter what the cost, even if it cost me my position as a minister of the Crown, should I fail in that duty, I would attemnt it and do the best I could, because I felt it was my duty to do it; and I must say that I trust hon. gentlemen opposite will be spared from having to take their lives in their hands to the extent to -which it was necessary to do so on that occasion, and to get in between two great fighting factions with a view to bringing them together. I do not wish to take any credit in the matter of bringing about a settlement in the Grand Trunk strike, but I do say that had it not been for the agencies which this government had established, had it not been that, in the first instance, the whole dispute had been made the subject of investigation by a board, so that when we came to a final adjustment it was a matter of taking the report of the board and sifting out certain features, and for the fact that there was existing, through agencies which the government had supplied, some means of bringing public opinion to bear on the whole situation, that strike, instead of lasting two weeks, might have lasted several months, and instead of being brought to a termination and of the men who were out being restored to their situations to the extent they have been, there might have been several hundreds who would never have got back their situations at all. My feeling is that had the government not intervened the result would have been disastrous all around, disastrous to the

Grand Trunk, disastrous to the men and still more disastrous to the general public. To the extent to which disaster of that nature has been averted, the government has rendered the country a service, albeit that there may be certain features in connection with that settlement that are not *quite as we would wish to have them.

House in committee on Bill (No. 75) respecting the McClary Manufacturing Company-Mr. Beattie.
Further consideration of section 1.
I suppose the committee have considered this Bill carefully, but it looks like a merger. Probably my hon. friend the Minister of Labour (Mr. King) has given thought to it.
What is the objection?

(There is a principle involved in the Bill. We have on the other occasions declined to allow mergers to be consummated in this manner. You see it gives to the company the power to purchase stock in other companies carrying on similar business. If that is allowed it permits in the very clearest way the possible consummation of a -merger among all the manufacturing industries in the same line. I am not quite sure that there is any strong objection to that but it seems to me that there is a principle involved, and that it would be well that it should come before a fuller House than we have to-night.

This is -a Bill introduce! on behalf of the McClary Manufacturing Company. The only persons interested in this company are the members of the Me

Clary family, and I think that you will find in the law as at present existing all that they are asking for. They have an establishment in every province of the Dominion, and agencies in different places, but instead of sending their own agents out on a paid salary to dispose of their goods they propose to entrust that work to persons in business in that line of goods in different towns and they ask for this power in order that they may be able to take some stock in their business. They think that by giving the sale of their goods to a business man in a town and then themselves taking an interest in the business he will push the sale of their goods more energetically, and will at the same time make a little money for himself. I have a statement explanatory of the Bill which, with the permission of the committee, I shall read :
The McClary Company were incorporated by chapter -116 of, the Statutes of Canada, 1882. The Companies Act, contained in the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906, and being chapter 79 of these statutes, contains clauses similar to the clauses in the McClary Bill. Fart 2 of the Companies Act applies to the McClary Manufacturing; Company. Section 122 of the Companies Act provides that Part 2 of the Act shall apply to every company incorporated subsequently to the 22nd day of June, 1869. by any special Act of the parliament of Canada. The McClary Manufacturing Company, being incorporated by special Act of the parliament of Canada in 1882. conies within the meaning of -this section. Part 1 therefore of the Companies Act does not apply to the MoCl-ary Manufacturing Company. If it did, section 44 gives -the right to purchase stock in other companies in a broader fashion than that in the McClary Bill. Section 44 permits a company, to -which part 1 of the Companies Act relates, to use its funds in the purchase of stock in any other corporation, when the directors have been expressly authorized by by-law passed by them for that purpose and sanctioned by a vote of not less than two-thirds in value of the capital stock represented at a general meeting of the company duly called for considering the subject of the by-law. You will notice, that in section 12 of the McClary Bill, it is provided that the directors must be authorized by by-law, sanctioned by a vote of not less than two-thirds in value of the subscribed capital stock represented at a general meeting duly called for that purpose, before they can use the funds of the company in the purchase of stock in any other company.
They -had a strike some years ago, and -an agent in a town refused to sell their goods on account of the attitude of the workingmen in the town, the result -being that he gave up the agency. The company had to take one of their own men -and start him selling the line of goods they manufactured. But their charter did not give them power to take any stock in his -business. That is why the Bill has -been brought forward. It has nothing to do with a

merger. Everybody knows that the Mc-Clary Manufacturing Company is one of the largest institutions of its kind in this country. It employs 1,300 men, and the stock is owned in the one family. They are merged in themselves in so far as that goes. I do not believe that they will think of merging with any other company. They are too large a concern for that, and their purpose for asking for this legislation is as it has been here explained.
I know the company very well, because they have a branch in my own city of St. John. I know they are a thoroughly respectable and exceedingly enterprising company.
Oh, very.

The only reason I rose was, that there would seem to be a principle involved in this first section. If we pass it as it is, it may be difficult to refuse similar powers to other companies, which were ostensibly seeking to create mergers, and it is giving parliamentary recognition to the principle that it is quite right for mergers to be created in this way. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Beattie), desires to have the Bill go through as it is, I do not intend to press my views.
Would the hon. minister like to see the letter; it will give him the facts.
Yes, please send over the letter. The object, as I understand it, is to enable them to take an interest in another company, which might qct as agents for the sale of their goods,

That is entirely the object of the Bill. They have an agent in almost every city at the present time, and instead of sending out an agent, they thought it better to take a firm who is in business in a certain place, and give them entire control of their productions there. The McClary company is. very extensively engaged in the manufacturing business, and they thought it would push their business better and lead to greater enterprise if they adopted this system. The McClary firm as every one knows, is an old firm, a wealthy firm, and a respectable firm.

I do not press my objection, Mr. Chairman.
