With reference to the question raised by my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) before recess regarding pensions on the Grand Trunk railway, I said that my impression _was that during the discussion between the parties, at the time of the negotiation, the matter of pensions was not mentioned, but the leader of the men declared that in that matter it was a matter of indifference to them what attitude, the company might take. I took occasion during recess to look up one or two documents, and I find in the Toronto 'Star,' of August 4 last, the following interview given to a 'Star' reporter by Mr. Murdock, who was one of the representatives of the employees concerned:

subtopic: PENSIONS DON'T BOTHER THE MEN, SAYS MR. MURDOCK-'TWAS A GIFT OF THE COMPANY AND MEN LOSE NOTHING. THEY CAN DO WITHOUT IT.

speechtext:
'What about the restorations of the pensions?' Mr. Murdock was asked.
' We are not paying any attention to that pension talk,' was the reply. * It was not touched on in the final settlement, as you know. The aim of most of these pension schemes is to test the fidelity of the men to
the union. In the strike there it was easily seen what effect it had on the allegiance of the men to their union, was it not? If railways will pay proper wages to their men there will be no necessity for these pension schemes at all.
If the Grand Trunk sees fit to pension its employees for years of faithful service, well and good. If, now, after the strike it chooses to be vindictive, and to say ' because for fifteen days you left our service we will disregard all your years of faithful work, and cancel your pension,' well, we have nothing to say as to that.'
In the Toronto ' Globe ' of August 5, I find the following interview of Mr. Berry, who was the representative of the other organization involved in the strike:

The object of Mr. Berry's visit to Montreal is to meet in conference with Mr. Murdock and the other strike leaders, and to go over the terms of settlement with a view to issuing an official explanation to the men. Also to arrange about the strike pay, and generally wind up the strike campaign. Mr. Berry was accompanied by Messrs. Todd, Dodge and Curtiss.

' I am not particularly concerned about the pensions,' said Mr. Berry, in response to another query. ' I believe that the company have the option of granting or refusing them. I have always looked upon pensions as a fake devised to deceive the workers. I believe in the men receiving a proper salary and being independent of any consideration such as pensions.' Mr. Berry also expressed himself as satisfied with the way in which the men were being taken back. He was not surprised at what the company officials were saying, and he dismissed their arguments with the advice to the men and the public not to take any notice of what the company said.
This came as a surprise to me. Messrs. Garretson & Lee, who were negotiating for the men, did not bring up the question of pension at all, and the other leaders took a stand in conversation, not unlike what they appear to have publicly taken in the interview I have quoted here. Speaking this afternoon my remarks may have seemed to imply that Messrs. Garretson & Lee also took the same stand in regard to pensions. I am not quite sure in regard to that, it may be they said nothing about that. As to the other men, dealing so far as Canada is concerned, the position they took was similar to the position they gave out in these interviews to the public.
In regard to the Springhill strike, to which reference was made by the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Rl*odes)J while the strike took place notwithstanding the report of the board which investigated it, nevertheless, the report of the board has had an effect on the situation which ought

to be helpful at the present time, in bringing the matter to a termination. The three members of the board were, Mr. Justice Longley, of Halifax, Mr. Archibald, of Halifax, and Mr. E. B. Paul, M.P.P. They agreed in the following, before the strike took place:
Under the circumstances your board cannot help recognizing that the only rational policy to be pursued by all parties concerned, is one of conciliation and forbearance in order that this large and important industry may not be compelled to cease operations, with most far-reaching and disastrous consequences to all, including the business men of the town. Hea?y loses have been already entailed by twenty-two strikes which have exhausted the energies and wasted the resources of the company.^ In the judgment of the hoard, the present is not a time to agitate for changes, but rather a time a common effort should be made to improve the situation and securo the permanence of the industry.	_
Your board saw tokens during the somewhat lengthy investigation of the matters in dispute that unpleasant feelings, if not distinct hostility, existed between a large number of employees and the management. It would perhaps be invidious to attempt to place the responsibility for this, but the hoard feel it their duty to bring this state of affairs to the attention of the directors of the company in a formal manner by means of this report.
This hoard recommends the directors to make a careful investigation into this unpleasant feature of existing relations with the hope that they may be able to adopt such a policy or make such changes as will prevent the possioility of this unfortunate condition prevailing in the future.
In this report of the board then, attention was drawn to the fact that it was an inopportune time to bring on the strike, and if a strike did take place, it was likely to last a long time, and do considerable injury to the community, and also that evidently there was something in the personality -of those who had to do with the management of affairs, that was in part responsible for the continuous friction, and the board suggested that the directors should look into that matter. The directors have looked into this, and I understand that the former manager is no longer manager at Springhill, his position has been filled by the appointment of Mr. Butler, formerly deputy Minister of Railways and Canals, in connection with this government. Therefore, in so far as the element of personality may have had an influence on the situation-and my own opinion is altogether in accord with that of the board, and also with that of Mr. Acland, who later investigated the situation-that factor has been removed, and it would therefore seem that the present is at least an opportune time for the men who may he still out, to go and negotiate with the new manager, Mr. Butler, and see if it is not possible to come Mr. KING.
to some sort of a settlement. As I said this afternoon, I spoke to Mr. Butler only a day or two ago, and Mr. Butler said he would be glad to have a talk with the men who are out. He also said that he would like me to state, if I had an opportunity of doing so in public, that so far as he was concerned in the management of these mines, he would not yield on the question of recognition. I think it only fair, that the parties in the dispute should know that fact, that the manager has stated he will close the mines before he will yield on that point, and I feel that the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes), could not render a greater service to his riding than to go down there with the knowledge which he has of the situation, and see if it is not possible himself to point out to the parties involved what the meaning and the ultimate probable issue will be of their continuing as they are at present, without endeavouring to get together and end what has been altogether a lamentable industrial dispute.
Inasmuch as these two strikes at Spring-hill and on the Grand Trunk railway have been discussed a good deal, and attention has been devoted to them in this parliament, I think it is only right, in order to give the country and the members of this House, a true impression as to the service which the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act has rendered this country, that 1 should attempt to give the House, in a few words a statement of what has been actually accomplished under that Act. In the first place, I would draw attention to the fact that the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act was enacted about four years ago. During that time, there have been altogether 100 boards applied for under that Act. In 91 out of the 100 cases, which have been referred to boards for settlement, strikes have been prevented, and in only 9 cases have strikes ensued. In other words, this legislation has been the means of averting over 90 per cent of the strikes which would otherwise have taken place in the Dominion in industries in the nature of public utilities. There are two ways of verifying these figures. If we compare the record of disputes which took place in the industries in the nature of public utilities for the four years prior to this legislation, with the record which has since been enacted, it will he found that the statistics verify what is given here as the result of the operations of this Act, that, as I have already said, in the industries in the nature of public utilities over 90 per cent of the strikes have been averted. Then there is the actual showing based on the sworn statement of the parties. For ten years the department has been gathering statistics of strikes and lock outs in Canada. It has been possible from these

figures, and by comparison with similar statistics in other countries, to find the average duration of strikes. In Canada for the last 10 years the average number of working days lost in each strike amounted to something like 24. In some cases the strikes lasted much longer, in other cases a shorter time, but 24 days seems to be the average. The men involved in the disputes that would otherwise have given rise to strikes, numbered 99,542, in other words, almost 100,000 men have been involved in these disputes that have been settled by boards and in which no strike has taken place. If we assume that the average wage for the men employed in these industries thus affected was $2.50 a day, and that in the cases where there have been settlements had there been strikes, the strikes would have been of the same average duration as in the case of other strikes, there has been saved through this legislation to the workingmen of Canada, in wages alone, a sum not less than $5,972,520; or in round figures $6,000,000 has been saved in wages to the workingmen of this country through the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act. I am not just sure as to how one can calculate the amount saved in profits, but if we assume that an employer would receive in profits 10 per cent of the amount which has been spent in wages to his employees, then there has been saved to employers in profits, in round figures, something like $600,000. If we try to form an estimate of the value of goods that would have been produced with that amount of labour, and with the capital that would have been employed, the smallest figure at which it could be placed, would be something like $10,000,000. That is to say, had strikes taken place where settlements have been effected and had these strikes lasted twenty-four days, commodities to the value of $10,000,000 would not have been produced, which have been produced. So, taking the inside estimate, the amount that has been saved to the workmen in wages is $6,000,000, the amount which has been saved to the employer is $600,000, and the amount saved in commodities that have been produced which otherwise would not have been produced is $10,000,000, or in round figures, something like $16,600,-000_ has_ been saved to this country by that legislation, and I might add the total cost of administering the Act, including all the expenses of the boards, has not exceeded in these four years $80,000.
That, I would point out, is only the monetary side of it. These industries to which I have referred are industries in the nature of public utilities. They are industries upon which the other industries depend, they are industries upon which the happiness and welfare of the community
depend. Take the strike at Lethbridge a few years ago; there you had families freezing in their homes for want of coal. Take a strike on a railway and you have something that influences the whole community. In all these cases the community, and all that goes with it, in so far as its relation to the industry is concerned, has been saved the inconvenience and the loss which would otherwise have taken place. While attention has been drawn to the fact that we have had in Canada in the last four year's one or two very serious strikes one should not lose sight of the fact that there has been saved to this country the vast sum of money and the vast amount of disorder which are indicated by the figures I have already given.
There is one other feature that I want to note in connection with the working out of this legislation, and that is the result of strikes that have taken place after the boards have given their findings and where the findings of the boards have not been accepted by the parties. As members of the House know, the parties to an industrial dispute in the industries covered by this Act are not allowed to strike or to lock out until the matter has been referred to a board. If they are not satisfied with the ' finding of the board then they may strike or lock out, and the returns indicate that while in 91 cases they have not struck, but accepted the findings of the board, in nine cases they have struck, and it is interesting to ask what has been the effect in the cases where they have gone on strike. The records show that in every one of those cases they have either returned to work on the terms which the board had granted or upon terms not as good as those which the board had granted. In no case have the working men who have gone on strike in Canada since this legislation was passed obtained better terms in consequence of their striking than they would have obtained had they accepted at the outset the findings of the board. Then,
I think it will be interesting as well to note, the relative position of the different industries concerned.
That would indicate, as I understood the minister to suggest by reading it, that it would be wise for the employees in all cases to accept the finding of the board in so far as experience has gone?

That is decidedly the opinion I have. My feeling is that this parliament, by enacting this legislation, has provided a better means of securing what is fair and just to the workingmen than it is possible for them to get in consequence of a strike. I do not say that the findings of the board are always the best thing that could possibly be obtained, but I do think
.'(399

and I say this, as a result of a careful watching of the industrial disputes which have taken place in Canada in the last ten years, the workingmen will gain more in the long run by accepting the findings of the board than by going out on strike.
The impression of the minister is that the Act has been successful in its operation from one view point. What is the view point of the labour men of the country?
I think the labour men of the country will agree absolutely with what I am saying at this moment.

I think the minister has an idea of what I refer to. I do not know that he has received them, but, speaking for my own constituency alone, I have received resolutions from all the lodges in the county calling for the repeal of the Act. Has the minister received any of these resolutions from Nova Scotia or elsewhere?

I am well aware of the^case to which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Rhodes) refers. Unfortunately, there has been, in the province of Nova Scotia, during the last year or two, a great deal of industrial strife. As the hon. gentleman knows that strife has come about largely through the endeavour of one union to get into possession and to be recognized, and the struggle that has been going on there has been largely between two different organizations rather than between employers and woTkingmen. -
That is true as affecting Nova Scotia, but has the minister received similar resolutions or requests from other provinces?

I am informed that all the communications that we have received of the nature to which my hon. friend makes reference have been from lodges of the United Mine Workers' Association, the organization that is concerned in the diffi-. culties in the province of Nova Scotia.
But have they all come from Nova Scotia?

They have come from the lodges of this organization in other parts of the Dominion, and it would appear therefore, that in so far as the united mine workers are concerned many of them are not satisfied with the Act. But, I would point * out that, while that is true, I know some members of the United Mine Workers' Association who are strongly of the opinion that the Act is the best piece of legislation that has been enacted in the interest of workers. There is a difference of view between them in that regard, but I can refer my hon. friend to the stand taken by the Dominion Trades and Labour Congress which represents the union has Mr. KING.
pretty generally in \the Dominion and which body strongly endorsed this legislation, and also to the communications which I read to this House last year from the representatives of the several railway organizations in the Dominion also endorsing this legislation.

I may say that in the report of the Deputy Minister of Labour with regard to conditions in Nova Scotia he pointed out that politics enter quite largely into the trouble down there, and that is illustrated veTy forcibly Dy the fact that while the United Mine Workers' in Nova Scotia are entirely opposed to the Act, and are calling for its repeal, the other body of organized labour, the provincial Workingmens' Association are taking a stand in its favour, but, it is interesting to note that while this organization is now at war with the United Mine Workers', at a meeting in Halifax in 1907, the Grand Council of the Provincial Workers' Association unanimously passed a resolution calling for the repeal of this Act in so far as _ it affected the province of Nova Scotia. While the minister is discussing this question I may say that the great grievance they have in so far as the Act is concerned is that there is no compensating feature in the Act to make good the loss to the men of the thirty days which they must work before they can go on strike. Under the Act there is no compensation coming to them at all. It simply means that the management receives 30 days' notice that there is going to be war which means that the management is able to fortify itself and consequently the efforts of the miners by means of a strike prove largely abortive, after the 30 day period. That is the great difficulty.
If my hon. friend had read the Act carefully he will see that the company is not allowed to change the conditions during that time.
Unfortunately they do.

If they do, then my hon. friend and those interested in the welfare of the men should point to the clause of the Act which gives the men redress, and under which the companies are liable to prosecution if they take steps of that kind. The Hillcrest Coal Company of Alberta did lock out its men on one occasion without giving notice, and they were fined under the Act.
How much were they fined?
I really forget at the moment.

That is all right if it is a lockout, but if the company should choose to say that they closed down be-

*cause business was dull, or because the plant calls for alterations and so on, it is a simple matter to have, in effect, a lookout.

Granting all that, they would have that power if the Act was not on the statute-books at all. But what the Act does give the workingmen which they never had before is the right to put their own man on the board, and he has the power to summon before him the members [DOT]of the company by which those whom he represents are employed, to examine their books, and get a complete statement before the public, in order to show who was right and who was wrong, and thus bring to bear upon the situation public opinion properly shaped and properly defined which is of all factors the strongest in bringing about justice in these industrial [DOT]disputes.
Mr- MADDIN. Does the minister wish the House to understand that employees may summon their employers to disclose their books, their sources of revenue, their cost of manufacture, their market price, and lay it before the public. I am sure he must know that the members of the board alone can receive that, and that they are worn to secrecy. The public are not *allowed to know that .and quite properly they should not know it.
What I stated was this-
The Minister of Labour [DOT]did say that this Act empowered workingmen - to appoint one of their own number to the board.
Yes.
To summon their employers and have the employers produce their books?
Yes.
And lay it before the public?
No, I did not say that.
The Act does not make any such provision, and it would be very unwise if it did.

I have the Act before me, and it provides, just what I said, that a body of workingmen, where a board is granted, may name any workingman they please,_ provided he has not a financial interest in the dispute, to represent them on the hearing, and that man once appointed has all the powers of a judge in the matter of summoning an employer, compelling him to produce his books, to show what profit he is making, what wages he paid, what is his output, and all the rest of it. This is the power under the Act, and it is a great power to give to any body of men ;
*a power very much greater than that of simply going out on strike and waiting while they are losing their wages day by day to see whether their endurance is stronger than that of some great corporation. I think that an enlightened view of the industrial situation will lead one inevitably to see that strikes are the last thing in the world which workingmen want. If there is any means whereby justice can be secured to the parties without that extreme measure, it should be resorted to. The record which I have given to the House to-night goes to show that our legislation which was inaugurated by this parliament as a whole, has done very great .service to the working classes, and to all .classes in this country. To cite only one instance in addition, take the case of street railway strikes. In the period of four years before this Act was passed there were six or seven strikes on the Street railways of Canada, and they were among the worst we had in the Dominion. They entailed considerable loss, and the community suffered very considerably. Now, since this Act was passed there have been seven boards in the large cities, Ottawa, Toronto, Hamilton, Winnipeg and Vancouver, and there has been only one street railway strike in four years, that being the strike which took place in Winnipeg a few weeks ago, when the men did not accept the award. The result of that strike is well known to the House. There is a concrete instance, taking only one industry, showing the immense service this legislation has been not only to the workers but to the public as well. I think that is a matter with regard to which we can afford to have a little national ipride.
I should like to put on record a comparison between the effect of our legislation, and the effect of the legislation in New Zealand, and New South Wales. A great deal has been said in the world at different times about the effect of the legislation in both these countries where compulsory arbitration laws exist ; it is sometimes said that there are no strikes there, and that they have found a panacea for these industrial difficulties which no other nation has found. When Mr. Beddoe, our Canadian trade commissioner went to New Zealand, I asked him if he would let me have a report in regard to strikes there in so far as he could get information and verify it on the spot. On August the 22nd last in a report which he sent to the department he gives a list of 16 strikes as having occurred in New Zealand within the preceding 18 months. If you make an allowance for the difference in population between the two countries, the strikes in New Zealand would amount to under their system of compulsory arbitration, 96, as
34U3

compared with 69 in Canada during a corresponding period. We had only 69 strikes in 1908, and if they had the same population they would have had 96. It is also of interest to note the effect of the enforcement of their law. Under the compulsory arbitration law the means resorted to by the state is to penalize employers, and employees when they do not abide by the findings. Suppose we had a similar law in Canada the effect would have been as follows : Had prosecutions for infringement occurred in Canada to a degree proportionate with the larger population of the Dominion there would have been during the last fiscal year no fewer than 9,672 employers, and 5,840 employees fined in our courts ; a total of 16,514 cases. This does not take into account the very considerable number of prosecutions in which convictions failed, so that it is not unfair to place the number of prosecutions on which the courts have been compelled to pass at 20,000. This comparison is made on the basis of 8 to 1 ; the population of New Zealand being in round numbers 1,000,000, and that of Canada 8,000,000. New Zealand has had 16 years experience of the Act, and this record obtains in the latest year, so that a country newly entering on similar legislation might reasonably expect to find the proportion of similar prosecutions higher. Then, New South Wales, which has also attempted legislation along compulsory arbitration lines, has had an experience hardly less satisfactory than that of New Zealand.
Mr. Harris Weinstock who was recently sent as a special commissioner from the state of California to visit Australia, in a special report with regard to New South Wales, states that the following figures as to strikes were given to him by the registrar of that State, having been taken from that officer's private file. In 1901, 2; in 1902, 12 ; in 1903, 11 ; in 1904, 11 ; in 1905, 36 ; in 1906 . 29 ; in 1907, 52 ; in 1908-in the first three months only-33.
, It is worth while comparing these figures for a moment, representing a state under compulsory arbitration, with the Canadian figures for the two years 1908-09, under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act. The strikes in Canada during each of those years were 69 only, a total of 138 for two years. The strikes in New South Wales for 1906 and 1907, two years nearest the Canadian years (the New South Wales figures for 1908 are incomplete, though very high so far as they go) totalled 81. The population of Canada is in round figures about five times that of New South Wales. Were our strikes proportionate in number with those of New South Wales they would have reached during the two years the very high figure of 405 or over 200 a year, a higher figure than has been shown Mr. KING.
in any of the ten years during which a record has been kept in Canada.
Has the minister any statistics to show the percentage of strikes before the enactment of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act as against those since?

Yes, certainly. The record has been kept in Canada for nearly ten years, and the statements that I have just been giving to the House are based upon the figures which are to be found in the annual report of the department; and if hon. members will take the trouble to verify what I have given to the House, they will find that since that Act passed we have in those industries to which the Act applies cut out some 90 per cent of^ industrial disputes by virtue of the legislation as compared with those which occurred before.	.	,
Just one further word m regard to the Grand Trunk strike to which my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) has referred. It appears that some hon. gentlemen opposite are endeavouring to hold the government responsible for all that has taken place since the settlement of that dispute. To give the government no credit, or as little as possible, for the settlement, but to make it responsible for everything not entirely satisfactory that has taken place since. In other words because two ministers were present and did their best to 'bring the parties together and to effect a settlement they would make the government liable for the carrying out of any agreement that might be arrived at under the operation of the Industrial Disputes Act. If the help of the state to bring about a settlement of an industrial disipute is to make the state responsible for everything the parties do in working out that settlement, that is imposing an unwarranted responsibility on the government and going_ a length which I do not think this parliament would approve. In November 1906 there was a serious strike at Lethbridge in Alberta. The mines had been closed for some months, and the people of the prairie provinces were facing a fuel famine at the beginning of the winter. I was sent out as deputy minister to try to effect an agreement between the parties. An agreement was arrived at upon every point except on the matter of discrimination as between union and non-union men. On that point a compromise was finally affected, both the men and the company agreeing to a clause which I drafted as representing, fairly I thought, the view of both. But we could not get the decision of the company for some little time after the men had given theirs, as to the acceptance of the proposed clause. After waiting some days, I

received the following telegram from the manager of the company :
The managing director still thinks our clause fair to all parties, but under circumstances existing in country is willing to accept your substitute clause provided all other conditions are accepted.
In reporting to this government on that settlement I made this statement:
I showed this wire to the representatives of the men with whom I had gone to Indianapolis, gave them an assurance in the name of the government that the company had accepted the clause which I had drafted and the conditions agreed to at the joint conference, and an hour later the strike was declared at an end.
I mention this case because it is a parallel one to xne intervention or the government in the settlement of the Grand Trunk strike. The parties to the Lethbridge strike had been negotiating for a settlement. The miners on the one side and the company on the other had come to a final agreement. It was an agreement between these two parties. But what the miners wanted was that the clause referred to should be known publicly to have been accepted by both sides; and I said to them, as an official who had been sent to endeavour to bring about a settlement:
I will vouch for that; I will see that there shall ; be no misrepresentation on that point ; and on that pledge being given, the strike was declared at an end. What happened? The mines opened up, work was resumed, and there was no further trouble there for some little time. But what hon. gentlemen opposite contend is that if some trouble had taken place subsequently, the government of this country should have ibeen held responsible, simply because an officer sent by the government had witnessed a term in the agreement, and was prepared to vouch for that being one of the terms ot the settlement. That is what hon. gentlemen opposite are attempting to do in the case of the Grand Trunk strike. -Now, the Grand Trunk settlement was arrived at between the parties themselves, Mr. Hays representing the Grand Trunk Railway Company on the one side, and Messrs. Garretson and Lee representing "?e on the.other side. These parties Tiir'i-J' 6 ne&otiating. The hon. Minister of Militia and myself spent two or three days doing our level best to get these parties to meet together, and when they did meet, to keep them together until they could arrive at some definite settlement. Feeling was running very high. The company had refused to negotiate with these leaders. Here is a telegram which I received from Mr. Murdock:
Messrs. Garretson and Lee held conference with. Mr. Hays to-day without result. '
The Canadian leaders had been trying to get a conference, but had been unsuccessful, and they sent to the United States for these two men, who were the heads of their organization, brought them to Montreal, and sought a further conference, but without any result. When Sir Frederick and I reached Montreal, that was the situation. The parties were unwilling to meet together, and we had to bring all the pressure we possibly could upon them to bring them together; and when we got them together we had to do our best to keep them together for a couple of days until we got the terms of the settlement threshed out. But the terms of the settlement were terms as between the parties themselves, not between the government of Canada and the Grand Trunk Railway Company or between the government of Canada and the men. We were there as ministers of the Crown prepared to vouch for the terms that were in that _ agreement should they ever be questioned. That position we are prepared to take up to the present. How was our action in that regard viewed by the men themselves? Let their own records speak. I have here a volume of the Railroad Trainmen of September, 1910. In an article on the Grand Trunk railway strike at page 297, there is the following:

The hon. minister has said that he and the Minister of Militia took an active part in bringing about a settlement, and I would like to ask him if he thinks that either of the parties broke any of the terms and conditions of the settlement arrived at ?

Well, I would say this, that if I had been one of the parties to the dispute, I would not have carried out the settlement in the way it has been, but every man can do as I have done, draw his own conclusion. I am prepared to state the terms of settlement, but every one is competent to judge for himself as to whether they have been carried out or not. In this article to which I have referred, I find the following:
The strike on the Grand Trunk railway system which was commenced July 18 under the direction of the Order of Railway Conductors and the Brotherhood of Railroad Trainmen, was ended on August 2 at six p.m., when the agreement was signed by Mr. Hays, for the Grand Trunk railway, and the committee of the Order of Railway Conductors and Brotherhood of Railway Trainmen for the men.
The strike was not ended by my colleague, the Minister of Militia and myself signing any agreement, but by this agreement being signed by President Hays and the representatives of the men. Here was the position at the time of the settlement,

a3 described in this article, by the leaders of these organizations : Referring to th^ situation prior to the settlement the article goes on to say :
The company, however, was able to secure enough strike breakers to enable it to run 148 freight trains within the 24 hours ending at six p.m., August 2, handling an average of 22 cars per train. While this average of trains run was far below normal conditions, a start had been made in the freight service, and it was only a question of time when the entire service would be resumed.
I would ask hon. gentlemen opposite, when they are endeavouring to saddle the responsibility on the government, of the non-reinstatement of some of the men-I think the number is around 200. out of a total of 4,000 involved in this dispute-to bear in mind this statement I have just read of the men themselves. According to this statement, it was only a question of time, when the entire service would be resumed by the company. I would ask hon. gentlemen opposite whether, in view of this statement, considerable service was not rendered to the employees by a settlement being effected. Instead of only about 200 men being out of employment to-day, there would have been considerably more had that strike been continued.
Passenger service on the main line was but slightly impaired at any time during the strike, while the branch passenger line service was demoralized for about a week.
That is what ' The Trainmen ' say. The article continues :
The settlement includes the return to the service within 90 days of every employee who left it with the exception of those who can be proven guilty of illegal acts against the company. The settlement was effected principally through the efforts of the Minister of Labour, the Hon. Mackenzie King, assisted by Sir Frederick Borden, Minister of Militia, to whom full credit is given for their efforts in bringing about the settlement.
My hon. colleague and myself 'are generously credited with having brought about a settlement, but the terms of the settlement were agreed to by the parties themselves. The parties, I believe, would not have got together, if we had not worked as we did, and the fight would have gone on until the railway company and the workingmen and the country as well, would all have suffered tremendous loss.
Then in the Railway Conductor's Magazine, published by the other organization, I find at page 718, the following:
In connection with this settlement, the thanks of the Canadian membership and that of our entire organization as well, are due and tendered to the Hon. Wm. L. Mackenzie King, Minister of Labour, and Sir Frederick Borden, Minister of Militia, for their untiring efforts in behalf of the men, for the Mr. KING.
influence they brought to bear upon ithe Grand Trunk Railway management contributed in no small degree in producing the satisfactory result and the ending of the controversy.
That statement goes to show that the efforts of the ministers contributed to bringing about a settlement, but the men themselves are responsible for the settlement finally reached.
Similarly, in a pamphlet issued on the Grand Trunk Railway Central Vermont strike, by W. G. Lee, president of the Brotherhood of Railway Trainmen, I find at page 10, the following statement:
The ministers of the Crown and particularly the Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, Minister of Labour, and Sir Frederick Borden, Minister of Militia, were largely instrumental in bringing about a settlement of the strike. They kept in close touch with the strike throughout its duration and made the most of every opportunity to bring the two parties together.
There was the service that we had been able to render, but the settlement had to be effected by the parties themselves, when they came together.
They are due high praise for their interest in the welfare of the striking employees and of those affected by the interruption of the company's traffic. Their efforts in behalf of the men are appreciated by both organizations and by officers and individual members of the brotherhood.
Then Mr. Garretson, president of the Order of Railway Conductors, sent the following communication from Cedar Rapids, Iowa, on August 10, to myself, and I believe sent a similar one to my hon. colleague, the Minister of Militia:
Cedar Rapids, Iowa,
August 10, 1910.

Mackenzie King,
Minister of Labour,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Sir,-I take this opportunity of expressing to you on behalf of not only myself and my associate officers, but of the organization at large and the more especially the Canadian membership thereof, the profound obligation under which we lie for the services of yourself and your associate minister in connection with the settlement of the strike upon the Grand Trunk and the Central Vermont railways. The ready recognition by you of the justification for the claims of the men on those properties and the exercise of personal and governmental influence toward securing a termination of the strike on those properties will not be forgotten by our membership and I sincerely trust that those most directly affected, namely, our Canadian citizens, will, in the future, make that appreciation thoroughly apparent.
In conclusion, kindly accept my expressions of highest personal regard, and believe me, Sincerely and gratefully yours, (Signed) A. B. GARRETSON, President.

1 would ask permission to read just one further communication, which I hope will be a satisfactory answer to my hon. friends opposite. This is signed toy Mr. S. N. Berry, vice-president of the Order of Railway Conductors, and James Murdoch, vicepresident of the Brotherhood of Railway Trainmen, and is dated, Windsor Hote' Ottawa, December 13, 1910
Windsor Hotel,	.
Ottawa, Dec. 13, 1910. Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King,
Minister of Labour,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-In further reference to conference held yesterday between the Premier, the honourable Minister of Railways and yourself with a committee of unreinstated Grand Trunk employees, accompanied by the undersigned, at which meeting the facts in connection with the Grand Trunk Company's failure to equitably apply terms of settlement made when strike was called off were discussed.
The committee desire to assure you, and through you the government, that they deprecate the attitude taken by certain gentlemen (presumably well intentioned) whereby an effort is being made to hold the government responsible for the failure to apply the terms of settlement made. .
I hope hon. gentlemen will keep that sentence in mind when they try to saddle on the government every failure on the part of either of the parties to live up to the terms of the settlement.
We appreciate fully the assistance given both at the time of the strike, and since, by the government in its efforts to bring about on behalf of the Canadian public and the citizens of Canada who were involved in the strike a settlement, and an equitable carrying out of the terms of that settlement. It is definitely understood by the men interested and the undersigned that it i,s not on account of any failure on the part of the government that the present unfortunate situation obtains, but that the existing conditions are rather the result of the obstinate disregard for contract obligations on the part of Grand Trunk officials.
The assistance given so far in a conciliatory and mediating way by representatives of the government is much appreciated, but the committee would further request that if consistent the government should take further means, if possible, either by the appointment of a Royal Commission or in some other consistent manner to enforce from the officials of the Grand Trunk an acceptable carrying out of the agreement made and understandings reached.
It appears to the committee that the government can consistently lend its further aid in straightening out this matter when the fact is recalled that the unreinstated Grand Trunk employees who are asking for the carrying out of the agreement made, are placed in such a position on account of the fact that aliens or American citizens who are present in charge of Grand Trunk affairs, have repudiated an agreement made with Grand Trunk 108
employees and an understanding reached with ministers of the Crown.
It is insufficient for those American officials to hide behind the statement that they have carried out their agreement as ' acts are more forceful than words ' and the facts are that more than 200 reputable Canadian citizens who have not been guilty of any overt act are being wrongfully held out of service to satisfy the vindictive and retaliatory desires of officers in charge.
We would again assure you that if the government can consistently arrange to take any further action in this matter either by the appoinment of a Royal Commission or other investigation, that the employees will be governed by any decisions reached as a result of such impartial investigation.
Will you kindly advise at your earliest convenience as to any further action taken or contemplated by the government.
We remain, very truly vours, (Signed) S. N. BERRY,
Vice-President O. R. C. (Signed) JAMES MURDOCK,
Vice-President B. of R. T.
There is the attitude that the men involved in this strike take towards the intervention of the government. And I must say that is the attitude I would expect workingmen, with the sense of honour that I know workingmen to have, to take, in view of the service that was performed. They know what was done to help in bringing about the termination of that strike, and, being grateful, they deprecate, naturally and rightly, the attitude of gentlemen for political reasons trying to make out that the government in some way is responsible for any incident or failure on the part of one of the parties to live up, in the way which might be expected, to the terms of that settlement.

I have something to deprecate too. I deprecate that the minister (Mr. King) should think it necessary to try to provoke difficulty for himself in getting his estimates through. He must be Irish, I think. He seems to throw down a challenge in order that a quarrel may be provoked. I would not speak at this time if it were not that the minister particularly challenged me by referring to me directly. The minister is on the wrong track. If I might use a vulgar expression which, probably, he would hardly appreciate, he is barking up the wrong tree.

I am not aware of having challenged the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lennox) in any way.
Mr.- LENNOX. The hon. gentleman (Mr. King) began his remarks with a reference to the hon. member for South Simcoe-I take it that he must have meant me.

If I may be allowed, I think the hon, gentleman misunderstood. Mv reason for mentioning the Grand Trunk



strike was that it was referred to before we got into Committee of Supply. In my remarks I did not have any personal reference to any member of the House whatever.

We will see. ' Hansard ' to-morrow will be our sufficient record as to what I say. The hon. gentleman (Mr. King) started by referring to the hon. member for South Simcoe, and he proceeded then to deal for a moment or so with the Grand Trunk strike. Then he wandered off to Lethbridge, and excused himself for that excursion by saying that the Lethbridge situation was illustrative of the position in the Grand Trunk strike. Then he wandered off to somewhere in the United States. I wrote a letter during the time he was discussing that matter, so cannot' profess to have followed what he said. But he did try to give the House the impression that hon. members on this side, notably myself as chief sinner, were attacking the government in reference to the Grand Trunk strike. Speaking for myself-and others can speak for themselves -I believe that all I have said about-the Grand Trunk strike in this House at any time has been in the form of two sets of questions put upon the Order Paper and the two or three questions that I asked this afternoon. And at that time I told the hon. gentleman distinctly through Mr. Speaker, who was then in the Chair, that I did not propose to pursue this matter until I had knowledge of the facts. The minister has thought fit to delay the passage of his estimates for several hours by bringing before the House-hoping, I suppose, to bring it before the country, but I do not think he will be successful in that- a lot of matter very eulogistic of the Minister of Labour. That we would naturally expect. Who can watch the course of the Minister of Labour and fail to be his admirer?-the gigantic work he is doing, and so on.

If the hon. member will pardon me, I would ask you, Mr. Chairman, if the number of members present constitute a quorum? I have seen estimates before Committee of Supply when there were more members on the government side.

The Minister of Labour (Mr. King) has not altogether emptied the House, and we can proceed. I would suggest to him that if we are to act harmoniously, he, at an early day, should discon-

tinue his practice of to-night. We would take it for granted, if the minister would let us do so, that he is doing well. I will take it for granted, at all events, that he is doing as well as he can-that he intends to do well. But it is not necessary that the time of this House should be taken up in placing on record, and thereby burdening ' Hansard ', with a lot of stuff that may prove to be mere twaddle to a great extent. The minister says he has the certificates of the men, and that they being actuated by a sense of honour, could not say anything else than that the government had done all it possibly could for them. The men have not spoken yet at all. Some representatives of theirs, who may or may not have acted well, have spoken, it is true. It is by the result of what I referred to this afternoon that we shall be able to judge whether these men did wrell or not. We cannot judge by these letters; we will judge by the facts and by the results. The minister is trying to crawl out of it already. He says the government are not responsible: they intervened, it is true, but the men must take the responsibility through their agents, for the government was not their agent- that, I think, summarizes what the minister says. But the men know that the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Militia intervened. That is a guarantee-or ought to be a guarantee-to the men that their interests will be-watched, and that they will not be thrown down. And if it turns out that the agreement entered into at Montreal between the representatives of the striking employees and the Grand Trunk railway was a gold brick; that the men thought they were getting an absolute and complete settlement of all difficulties, that the slate was being cleaned, that all differences were being removed, that they were being reinstated as if no strike had taken place, and that all would be reinstated except those guilty of violence-if it turns out that these men were thrown down, it will not redound to the credit of the government, but the government will be held responsible. That is what I want to say to the minister since he has challenged the position. And I want to tell him also that he intervened in this strike at a critical time. And he did not do much. All that he and the Minister of Militia did, as far as I can ascertain, was to get from the railway company finally a statement which they would not put in writing, that when they spoke of taking on these men as soon as possible, that meant that they would take them back within ninetv days. But what I am led to understand by the men themselves, whatever these representatives may have said to the minister, is that they believed when that strike was being settled by the intervention of the government that they were to be restored to the same

positions they stood in at the time the strike was called. If it turns out that that is not the case, I for one, and I have a right to speak of it in this House, whatever the agents may say, will say that the government is not without blame in the matter. If it turns out, on the other hand, as I hope it will, that these men were to have been secured in all their rights and the Minister of Labour did . not see to it that the agreement was broad enough to cover those rights, then too he will be responsible. If it can he placed in a better position than that I will be quite ready to say that I have no condemnation of the minister in that matter. I do not intend at this moment to make any charge of default on the part of the minister of any kind but, as I said this afternoon, when the proper time comes and when I have my facts, I will then, if they justify such a course, bring it up in the House.

In response to an inquiry which I made of the minister this afternoon as to why it was that he intervened in the case of the Grand Trunk strike, and not at Springhill, the minister has stated that in the former case he had a request, and in the latter he had not. Practically that summarizes the distinction between the two strikes. That he did not interfere in the case of the Springhill strike or tender his services for the purpose of mediating between the parties because he was not requested to do so. It seems to me that for that very reason the minister ought to intervene, and I say this with the utmost deference and good will, and because I have the interests not necessarily of my own constituents but of labouring men throughout the country at heart, and am prepared to believe that the Minister of Labour has their interests at heart as well. My contention is that if the Department of Labour is to be of full benefit to the people of this country it must exercise, if I may use the term, its plenary powers to go, and attempt to adjust differences wherever they may occur. If there is a fight on between individuals they get rather hot headed, they are not amenable to reason, and they battle away until one or the other-wins, it is a question of the survival of the fittest, and the man having the greatest brute force wins, but that does not necessarily mean that the better side wins. What is true of individuals is true of organizations and of nations. When two nations resort to the arbitrament of war, the nation having the greatest number of soldiers, and the greatest financial resources wins out, but it does not follow that the nation having the right side of the quarrel wins. In the case of industrial disputes, where the parties are at daggers drawn, as at Springhill, it is perfectly natural that they will not ask some third party to intervene.
I think the minister gave a very good reason why he should intervene in a remark he made with reference to the Grand Trunk strike. He said that no agreement would have been effected there had we, referring to himself and the Minister of Militia, not worked very hard. He goes to show by that fact alone that a third party coming in, not knowing either side of the dispute, and there only to bring the parties together, is able to accomplish a much greater work than can be done by the parties themselves. The minister was pleased to say that I could glorify myself if I could settle this strike. Allow me to say to him that there is a member of parliament covering every constituency in this Dominion, and that you could not have an industrial dispute without a member being affected. If you are going to place the responsibility of settling strikes on the members of parliament, why have a Minister of Labour at all ? Otherwise the duties of the department are simply clerical, they consist in getting statistics, and publishing the ' Labour Gazette ' which could be done by a staff of officials working under any other department. I did not like the attitude of the minister in attempting to make it appear that our efforts on this side were largely partisan. I did not see any attempt before the minister spoke on the part of members on this side to place the responsibility for the failure of the settlement of the Grand Trunk strike on the government.
I was not referring to anything that took place in the committee, I was referring to previous discussions in the House when I spoke of these things.

But a minister, a man clothed with authority, coming froim a long distance away, can do a great deal towards the settlement of a strike, whereas a member of parliament, who happens to be on the ground, who may know the conditions, who is himself a representative of some one_ political party has not the same opportunity of doing effective work as the man from the outside, or the man occupying a higher office. If the minister is to act as negotiator only in cases where he is called on, we might as well dispense with his services altogether, because the parties could call in a judge or a member of parliament or a clergyman or a professor ; but if we are to have the full benefit of a labour department, we should have a minister or a deputy or some competent man in the department prepared, wherever there is a labour dispute of any dimensions, to go to the scene of the trouble and stay there until a settlement m some form or another is effected.
I hope that the minister will see his way clear without a request to go down to Springhill, and I may say that if there
341a

is anything I can do I should 'be very happy to go along with him, because I believe in the interests of the men who are struggling there to-day, in the interests of the country, and of the community at large, if there is a possible means of settling that strike, it ought to be settled.

The Minister of Labour in his speech to-night has gone to some trouble to paint a very good picture of the Minister of Labour. Lord Macaulay, in his essay on Warren Hastings, describes a distinguished gentleman who sat to Lely the painter, and who said to him: Paint me as I am; if you leave out one scar or pimple I shall not pay you a penny. I am quite sure that when the distinguished gentleman who occupies the portfolio of labour had finished adorning himself tonight he had such a halo around his head as would astonish Michael the Archangel. He decked himself with a wreath that contained everything from roses to sunflowers.
I would like to add to that wreath one thistle-only one-and I take it from a fellow countryman of his own, a good Scotch Liberal fellow newspaper man in the province of Nova Scotia. True his political faith was not always as good as it is at the present time. I refer to the Hon. Robert Drummond, member of the legislative council of Nova Scotia, and publisher of the maritime ' Mining Record.' There appears in an issue of that paper an article referring to a description of the Minister of Labour published in the Canadian ' Courier,' and I am quite sure that the minister cannot be held responsible for observations contained in the ' Courier.' But, these are the deductions and conclusions that the Hon. Robert Drummond drew from this article and published in his paper last August. He said:
The * Canadian Courier ' in an article highly eulogistic of Hon. Mackenzie King refers to him as the * boy minister.' No one dares to criticize any of Mr. King's actions without a swarm of liberal press bees swooping down on him. This raises a doubt in the minds of some, as to Mr. King's alleged towering abilities. If in the Department of Labour he has been a towering success, his works are all the praise he should need. We in Nova Scotia are not in a posi tion to fairly criticise the boy minister. He has never shown us any of the tricks of his department. Perhaps we did not give him the right opportunity. We did give him one opportunity but then it may not have been to his liking, and that perhaps accounts for his not making much of a fist of it. Indeed the boy minister acted in a way which could not be called other than boyish. There was a strike at Springhill and Mr. King came all the way from Ottawa to fix it up. On coming to the junction he found that Mr. Cowans was in Halifax. Instead of taking the next train to Halifax he sent a long telegram to Mr. Cowans and took the next train back to Ottawa. So like a boy.

Why did'nt he telegraph to find out if Mr. Cowans was at home before taking so long a journey. Was it because he was a boy and inexperienced that Laurier sent Sir Frederick to assist Mr. King in the Grand Trunk Railway strike. What is the use of beslobbering the boy over the settlement; any one with ordinary brains could have done all that the minister did with the government at his back. By and by when Canada grows bigger the Department of Labour will need a heavyweight. By that time Mr. King's boyhood days may be over and by age and experience he may be fitted for so ticklish a post. Give Mr. King an open field and no favour, but for pity's sake don't say he is a wonder because he does the work of his office to the best, of his ability.
And, Mr. Chairman, with the canniness of a Scotchman, Mr. Drummond would not continue by saying ' and that is not saying much.' In his eulogy of himself this distinguished gentleman to-night told us that he hoped hon. gentlemen opposite would not be obliged to take their lives in their hands as he had been. He did not indicate whether it was his physical or his political life. He told us since dinner that he had gone out to Lethbridge during the strike there when people were dying. He crowns himself with everything he can bedeck himself with, he makes himself a great hero indeed; in fact, I wondered how it was that he did not come back from Lethbridge with the Carnegie medal for heroism, or something of the kind.
However, Mr. Chairman, this distinguished gentleman has told us to-night about the strike situation in Nova Scotia, and he has given us the reasons why he did not intervene at Springhill. He was discreetly silent with regard to the county^ of Cape Breton, and with regard to the strike there in the constituency which I have the honour to represent. I would like to say that when the minister makes the statement that he made here to-night that the difficulty of the labour situation in Nova Scotia was due to a war between the two unions, he is not stating what is absolutely correct. When he was asked to-night if he had received petitions himself against the Industrial Disputes Act asking for the repeal of it, and said that he had, but that they came from the United Mine Workers of America, I would remind him that in September, 1907, when this Act had been taken up by the Provincial Workingmens' Association at Halifax at their annual convention, and after they had studied it in all fairness and all reason, they unanimously passed a resolution which was submitted to the then Minister of Labour, the present hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) who, I am pleased to see in his seat to-night, asking for the repeal of the Act. The Minister of Labour tells us that the strike situation has some political significance in Nova Scotia. I want to remind

Mm again that before the United Mine Workers of America had taken up a position in Nova Scotia, and while that very resolution was receiving perhaps the due consideration of the Postmaster General, who was then the acting Minister of Labour, the miners of the Dominion Coal Company had a grievance, they called a special meeting of the council of the Provincial Workingmens' Association, that convened at New Glasgow, and who did the lobbying? The very gentleman who eulogizes in such a beautiful manner the Minister of Labour, the Hon. Robert Drummond, was on the scene. Not only did that special meeting of the grand council of the Provincial Workingmens' Association ask for a board of conciliation, but under such special auspices as they had on that occasion and with delegates from amongst the employees of the Intercolonial railway, from amongst the employees of Halifax and Truro, the miners of Cumberland, Pictou and Inverness, but they undertook to discuss, compare and study the Nova Scotia statute which has reference to arbitration, and the Industrial Disputes Act. Not only did they settle in favour of the Industrial Disputes Act, but these gentlemen from the various lodges undertook to name their representative on the board to represent the employees of the Dominion Coal Company, and with Mr. Drummond outside manipulating the discussion there was named Dr. Arthur Kendall, M.P.P., who sits on the Liberal side of the legislature of Nova Scotia. There was no United Mine Workers' in Nova Scotia then. I would like, however, to point out that the protests that came at that time from the Provincial Workingmens' Association have been followed since by protests from the United Mine Workers of America, numbers of which I have received from day to day, and some of which I have here in my hand to-night. I wish to say I have every sympathy with the Minister of Labour with regard to a situation of that kind. He talked about taking his life in his hands. I am prepared to take my political life in my hands and to stand w ith the Minister of Labour for the preservation of the Act if he will amend it, so as to make it a reasonable working Act. I wish to repeat, in order to make myself plain, that I am not in favour of the repeal of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, but I do wish the minister would take steps to render it more effective in practice and to remove the objections to it. I realize that this is new legislation, embarking in a new field. It is a new industrial tribunal, as it were, and naturally it is not a perfect one. The Canada Temperance Act, when it was passed originally in 1868, was over-burdened with imperfections, but in 1908-and I think as a lawyer I am safe in saying it-it is one of the most perfect pieces of legislation
to be found on the statute-books of Canada. And how was that brought about? As breaches of the Act arose, as offenders escaped the penalties of the Act, parliament amended it and by amending it perfected it. And in the light of our experience with the Industrial Disputes Act, I believe it could be so amended as to make it acceptable to employers and employees alike. I am not one of those who, if I build a dike to secure my lands from the overflow of the river and find that notwithstanding my efforts the water had inundated my lands, would say: Destroy the dike. No; I would seek the weak spots; I would look to the holes in it; I would repair these, strengthen the work, and try to make it a perfect dike. If the minister will seriously take up this Industrial Disputes Act, if he will follow the counsel given by the leader of the opposition in the resolution he moved in 1907, and which was talked out at six o'clock by the member for South Cape Breton of that day; if the Minister of Labour will take the counsel offered in that resolution to consult the employers of the country, and to consult the employees and labou? unions of the country and get them together and have each side point out the imperfections of this Act, I believe he would be able to secure a more perfect piece of legislation than we have at present. Surely there can be no objection to such a course as that. The minister Quoted statistics, and if we accept his figures (and figures can be made to serve almost any purpose) 91 per cent of the disputes that have arisen under this Act have been settled without a strike, and the remaining 9 per cent have been settled according to the decree of the board, or on terms less acceptable to the men who had asked for the board. Let me point out to the minister that this law was enacted in 1907, and since that year the cost of living has been going up in an ascending scale. From whom would the demand come for a conciliation board? I asked him if he would furnish this House some time with the percentage of the number of requisitions from employers and employees/. I will venture to prognosticate that 90 per cent of these petitions emanated from employees and not employers. Above all other times this is a time when employees should be receiving increased wages. This is a time when the cost of living is greater than ever before, and consequently the men must ask for an increase, and when they are refused they are met with this Industrial Disputes Investigation Act. They dare not strike until they get the board, and how do they get the board? They must ask for it. But is that all? No, Sir. They must accompany their application with a sworn statement that unless the board is granted there will be a strike. Is not that a beautiful

piece of legislation? Doesn't it encourage strikes? What are the men to do when the board decides against them? They are compelled, first of all, to swear that they will strike unless the board is granted, and when the board gives a decree that is not acceptable to them every principle of manhood forces them to make good the statutory declaration which they are compelled to send along with their application for a conciliation board. Let me tell the minister that it would be very interesting, to this House to have statistics to show how often the employer met the request of the employees when they presented their petition to the Department of Labour; how often they met it in a conciliatory way, and how often they stood aside and said: The men have no case, and we won't appoint anybody. The Act provides, in that case, that the government shall appoint a representative of the company. This forces upon the department a species of patronage which I have no doubt is quite distasteful to them. It forces them to look for some one to represent the corporation, and what is the re-, suit? We are told that politics creeps into these things at times. Is it not a fact that that corporation wherever it may be situated, from Vancouver to Sydney, or from the Great Lakes to the Arctic ocean, will invariably, through its representatives, proceed to Ottawa and say: We won't have anything to do with this board, and whilst under the statute it becomes your duty to appoint a man to represent us, you must be mighty careful whom you appoint. There is appointee No. 1, by the government, after the precautionary measures taken by the employer. What follows: The corporation, or employer, then goes to its representative appointed by the government and says: Don't you agree with the other representative as to a chairman. Don't you dare do it; you are appointed to represent us; we are very reluctant to have anything to do with this thing, but we instruct you now as our representative to be very careful; you must not agree on the third man. Then, under the law, at the end of five days it is up to the government again to appoint a chairman, and it is then the pressure is brought and that the representatives of corporations all over the country get around the department and say: You must be mighty careful in the appointment of the chairman.

Will my hon. friend allow me to make a statement? While he is throwing out such suggestions as he is doing now I may say that in at least 60 per cent, or probably more, of the cases the parties themselves have agreed on a chairman. During the time I was deputy minister, I think there was one occasion when a corporation suggested to me the name of a man whom they would like as a chairman. I told the person who suggested Mr. MADDIN.
it to me very plainly that that man certainly would not be appointed, and that hereafter I would thank them if they minded their own business. No corporation and no individual has ever approached me since I have been minister, or brought any kind of pressure to bear as to who the chairman of the board should be, and any corporation or individual who ever does may expect to have his or its name publicly disclosed.

The hon. minister has stated his position in matters of this kind, but I wish to tell him that he will spend a good many nights and Sundays_ before he will be able to disabuse the minds of the employees throughout the Dominion of Canada that where the government is vested with the appointment of two members of a board of conciliation the men are going to get a square deal from that board. The workingmen of this country know the power of corporation influence, and whilst the hon. minister cites one particular case, he does not give the name of that case. Then, he tells only of one instance where one of the parties affected, came to him. I wonder if he will go into the confessional now and tell us how often he was approached by members of this parliament who counselled him as to making appoints ments either as representatives of constituents, of their own, or as members of a board.

I have consulted with the members on both sides of the House, with regard to members of boards. I am not aware of a single member of the House having come to me to ask me to appoint a single man to a board.
Will the hon. minister go a step further and tell us the names of some of the members on this side of the House whom he consulted ?
I cannot think of a name at the moment, but I think I can give him one or more.

The hon. the minister thinks if he had time he could name one man. When it comes to the selection of a chairman, the government appoint him. I say this, without any apprehension of successful contradiction, that when a government which makes appointments of postmasters, harbour commissioners, overseers of fisheries and rivers and streams by the score, and makes appointments such as this government makes, which appoints men that have nothing to do, but draw their salaries-and their name is legion-I ask the hon. minister if he thinks the common labourers of this country are going to accept as bona tide, a tribunal so constituted that two out of three of its members are appointed by this government ?

I have no hesitation in saying that I think the workingmen generally know that the appointments made have been eminently satisfactory, and that the hon. gentleman will be unable to cite a single instance where any chairman of any board or any appointee of the government has given ground to any one to believe that he has done other than fill his position honourably and fairly and in the best interests of all parties concerned.
I have not made a study of all the cases under this- Act; they are not compiled and put into a volume which one can see in a law library. They appear only from time to time in the ' Labour Gazette.'
They are all compiled in the annual report.
Not by themselves. They are overwhelmed with a lot of rubbish.
No, by themselves.

I have not followed the decisions of conciliation boards in other provinces, but I am familiar with a number of those which have been given in the province of Nova Scotia. I do not complain particularly of any one who has acted, either as an appointee of the government or on behalf of a corporation, from my own personal knowledge of the gentlemen who have acted on conciliation boards in Nova Scotia. I am presenting to the minister complaints with which the labouring communities are pregnant, and which you will meet with on every hand, and the natural deductions which thoughtful men will draw from the decisions of tribunals so constituted as these * conciliation boards are at the present time. A dispute between the employees of the Dominion Coal Company and that company arose in the county of Cape Breton in the spring of 1909. A board of conciliation was applied for, and it sat during the month of April. While the board was sitting at Glace Bay. and witnesses -were going up and testifying as fo the discrimination against them on account of the union they belonged to, after Mr. Mackinly Cameron, a barrister of Glace Bay, presenting the case on behalf of the men, had called 15 witnesses who swore that on the morning after the night they joined the United Mine Workers of America, their lamps were stopped and they were refused employment, and when Mr. Cameron asked: 'do you think it worth while to call any more witnesses ?' Mr. Duggan, the vice-president of the company, said: * 1 will admit that there was discrimination, but it was without the knowledge or consent of the company, and the company regrets it, and will put an end to it,' While the board was sitting, over 500 men in the
employ of the company had been dismissed for no other reason than that they had joined the United Mine Workers of America. What happened ! If it had been a trial before the Supreme Court, the company would have been brought before the bar for contempt. It demonstrated its intention throughout the whole proceeding, not to be bound by any finding .of the beard, because, while the board was sitting, it went on erecting an eight foot fence, miles in length, surrounding its property, and stringing over it three strands of wire, carrying about 1,000 volts on which it put up notices: ' Danger, live wire.' This was done while the board was considering whether or not the company was discriminating against its employees. With the statement of Mr. Duggan, that there would be no further discrimination, those men returned to work. Matters went on smoothly for some time, and the number of 500 went up by the first of July to 900, and on the 6th of July the men called a strike-not for recognition of the union. You cannot put your finger on a single published utterance, or find a single officer of the United Mine Workers of America, from its president, T. L. Lewis, in the United States, or the president of district No. 26, in the province of Nova Scotia, Mr. Dan Macdougall, dowm to the president of the humblest local union in the province, who demands recognition. But what they did say, and what they had a right to say, wa;s this:
' You had no right to dismiss us, or any one of us, for joining the labour union of our choice.' I ask the hon. minister if he concedes to the people -of this country, what our statutes have afforded them, what has been made an exception to the law of conspiracy, namely, the right to form labour unions ?
Certainly.

The moment that is conceded he must agree with me when I say that labour in this country has the right to choose its own labour institutions and not the organizations which are the choice of the employers. That being the case it would be much better if the minister would deal equitably with the situation such as we have in Nova Scotia. It would be much better if he would deal fairly and frankly with the men and not take his version of the situation from this report which was furnished by his deputy under circumstances which I intend to speak of later on. It would be much better for him not to take his views from the columns of the ' Globe ' and of newspapers in Nova Scotia anxious fo make out that the strike was originated for the purpose of serving political ends. I would ask that he would deal fairlv with the situation there rather than believe that the strike was for the recognition of a union.

Wanklyn, vice-president of the Dominion Coal Company, is in Ottawa to-day. He came .up from Montreal last evening and immediately got into communication with the Militia Department. He was informed as to the procedure necessary for the despatch of troops to protect the mines at Sydney and was advised that a requisition from the municipal authorities or the county judge to the district officer commanding w'as all that was required. This was secured from Judge Fin-layson. This morning Mr. Wanklyn received a message stating that the special military train bearing the Royal Canadian Regiment at a strength of 512 had left Halifax at 3.45 a.m. The despatch added that things are quieter this morning but that some tracks were dynamited last night and a rifle shot fired at No. 6 colliery. I think the arrival of the troops will end it all, stated Mr. Wanklyn this morning. My advices are that only 33 per cent of the men are on strike and most of these are unskilled labourers.- We propose to fight them to a finish.
Further on the despatch says:
Mr. Wanklyn had a further conference with the acting deputy Minister of Militia this morning and afterwards called upon Sir Wilfrid Laurier. He explained that his visit to the Premier was wholly personal and to advise him of the conditions in which he is naturally interested.
On the morning of the 6th of July we had a strike down in Cape Breton, and on the following evening there arrived in Ottawa the vice-president of the Dominion Coal Company, Mr. Wanklyn, who called, not on the Labour Department-no, but on the Minister of Militia, to tell him that the company were going to fight to a finish. Naturally, under the circumstances, he .called on the Militia Department and not on the Department of Labour.
In what year was that?

In 1909. Mr. Wanklyn had come up to Ottawa for the purpose of consulting (the Minister of Militia and not the Minister of Labour. Mr. Wanklyn was' going to fight the men to a finish.
The hon. Minister of Labour has properly said that the last thing people want is a strike. He could picture the horrors of it, as I have seen them myself, time and time again before there ever was an Act on our statute-book.
