The men themselves do not want to strike, but I want to say to the minister that when he takes out of the hands of the labouring men of this country the only weapon they have effectively to enforce their rights and gives them no compensation, he is putting himself in a position which is anything but enviable.
I hope my hon. friend does not intend to imply that anything of the kind is done.
Absolutely.
Nothing of the kind is done. The right to strike is not taken away in any manner whatever, but the parties have to wait until the statute is acted upon.

That is an argument and an aspect of the case with which I propose to deal. But how does the Act work? The men say they have a grievance and the Act operates in the interests of the employers and not of the employees. The men want an increase in wages which the employers refuse to give, and the men require that increase to meet the increased cost of living. They must send their application to Ottawa and accompany it by an affidavit declaring that there will be a strike unless their demands are conceded. The minister has five days within which he must notify the opposite party. When the opposite party has been served with a notification, it must reply in five days and then it has five days within which to appoint a representative. And these two have five days more in which to agree on a chairman. If they do not agree within the five days, the Department of Labour or the Governor in Council appoints a chairman. In this way over thirty days may elapse before the' board is constituted. Then the board sits, and after they have arrived at a conclusion, if it be not satisfactory, the men dare not strike until another thirty days. What could work better, in all conscience, in the interests of the employers than just such a provision? We have an alien law so loose and easily handled that from across the borders are brought strike breakers. That was done in the Canadian Pacific Railway strike, four or five years ago, in the Grand Trunk Railway strike of last summer, and in the strikes of the Dominion Coal Company and in Cumberland county, and that will continue to be done so long as the government is so

partial to the employers as to have this law on the statute-book which it is nobody's business to enforce.
In the particular case to which I have referred, what happened? While the board was sitting, the Dominion Coal Company were" building their miles and miles of eight foot fences and stringing their wires by coming in contact with which two little boys were killed. That is what the company was doing during the not less than sixty days' notice they had of a struggle against organized labour. And what had the employees to do during those 60 days? Dig coal every day:-a public utility, therefore they must serve the public and incidentally earn more dividends for their employers. They must not cease to work under a penalty of $50 a day for every day they were not working. And think of these men who had petitioned for a board of conciliation-last week they reached their work by crossing an open field; yesterday they had to go round the end of a fence; to-day they have to go through a gate in that fence. And shacks are thrown up to shelter imported labour; every hardware store is canvassed for stoves and cooking utensils. Here was the enemy-if the employer can be called the enemy of labour? though I do not see why that should be, and I would like to see employer and employee come together and adjust their differences-here was the enemy preparing for war, while the men were forbidden to make any preparations. They had to raise a bank of 400,000 tons of coal while the employers were raising the shacks to shelter the scab labour that was to beat them out in the end.
The minister did make some inquiry into these conditions in Cape Breton. He did send down the Deputly Minister of Labour. But before I speak of that, I want to go on with the story of how they got the militia into the county. Mr. Wanklyn came up here on the evening of Wednesday, the 7th of July. And on. Wednesday afternoon shortly after mid-day, application was made to the mayor of Glace Bay, to the mayor of Dominion and to the warden oi the municipality of Cape Breton, the company having coal mines in all these different districts. They refused to requisition the militia, and application was made to His Honour Mr. Justice Finlayson. And I wish to say here, as an aside perhaps, as it may not be strictly pertinent to this inquiry, that His Honour Mr. Justice Finlayson. sitting in the county court there, was obliged to try day after day many cases arising out of the strike, painful cases-distresses for rent, evictions from tenement houses and so on; they were ground out by the thousand. The application was made to Mr. Justice Finlayson for the militia. And, while there have been one or two who questioned his integrity
and fidelity to his office in the discharge of his duties on that occasion, I wish to say here to-night, on the floor of parliament, that as solicitor for the men, their chief solicitor at that time, L found Mr. Justice Finlayson absolutely honourable, upright, fair, courteous and obliging from the beginning to the very end. Now, application is made to His Honour Mr. Justice Finlayson for a requisition for the militia. He granted that requisition. And what then? I regret that the Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden) is not here, but they actually posted the orders at ten o'clock on Wednesday morning in Halifax-mobilization orders for the regular troops. The Militia Act only provides for the regular troops being called out in the event of the local troops being inadequate. Mobilization orders at Halifax, ten o'clock Wednesday; Mr. Wanklyn calling on the Premier, to inquire about his health, Wednesday afternoon and the Minister of Militia, or the acting deputy Minister of Militia. asking for forces. These were the steps taken to settle that labour difficulty, and so the troops came down to Cape Breton. And what now, do you suppose? They are actually charging the people of Glace Bay, Dominion and the municipality of Cape Breton thousands of dollars for the expenses of these members of the regular militia of Canada. Was there ever anything so outrageous on the face of the earth? Who is paying these men to-day? Do not the people of Canada pay them? But those who asked for them, or have their services reluctantly thrust upon them must pay for these soldiers. Had there been no strike in Springhill the regular troops of this country would have been paid. Annually the Minister of Militia takes his seat here and calls upon us .to vote the money to pay these men; it is voted by this House and the country pays it. Why, then, should the municipality of Cape Breton, or the town of Glace Bay, or the tpwn of Dominion pay for these men when their services are required on account of a strike or an invasion? However, the minister did show his hand in the situation in Cape Breton. He sent down his deputy to the county, and that gentleman made a report which came to hand in this House some time during the last year and a copy of which I have now before me. He says, referring to the strike at Springhill that there were several grievances referred to, one being that of recognition of the United Mine Workers of America, others relating to conditions of work. The hon. minister told us this evening that he did not wish to intervene in the situation at Springhill because there it was a fight for recognition of the union. But his deputy lays before this House a report in which he says that there were several grievances at Springhill, one of which was recognition

of the union What has the minister done to alleviate the friction in the other ease? The men were paid by the ' box ' and what constituted a ' box ' was well known to be one of the^ vital questions One board of conciliation decided that 1,700 pounds of coal should constitute a ' box But the company wanted to change that, making a heavier ' box ' That was one of the things that the men protested against. Another question was the schedule of rates in connection with the mine. I wonder did the minister do anything to alleviate the circumstances in this case? His deputy reports that there were several grievances, one of which was the recognition of the United Mine .Workers of America. And the minister washes his hands to-day and says: We could not intervene the whole question was that of recognition of the union. This officer proceeded to Sydney and spent some considerable time there-I do not know just how many days. But he gathered a good deal of information. He points out that there was a conciliation board held in March, 1908. That is the board I had reference to that was so ably constituted by Robert Drummond and Doctor Kendall at New Glasgow, and which was participated in by delegates from all over the province who were members of the Provincial Workmen's Association. He says:
It is to be noted in connection with the above list of men prominent in the agitation that Mr. MacDougall, now President of the District Council of the United Mine Workers of America, was a member of the sub-council of the Grand Lodge of the Provincial Workmen's Association in March, 1908, when the existing agreement between the Dominion Coal Company and its employees was concluded before a Board of Conciliation and Investigation established under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, and presided over by Professor Adam Shortt.
The deputy minister thinks it is his duty to incorporate in the report he lays before parliament the fact that the President of the United Mine Workers had actually signed and approved of a settlement, of a wage schedule between the employees and the company in March, 1908. Why, some newspapers in this country went so far as to say that the company could not deal with the United Mine Workers of America because they had a contract and they spell that contract in capitals in every Grit paper from the Halifax ' Morning Chronicle ' down to the Sydney ' Record.' They spelled it in capitals and they underlined it and put quotation marks around it and nursed it and nurtured it and held it up to the public and said: There is a contract, we cannot negotiate with these men because of. that contract. But the Deputy Minister of Labour knew there was no contract, there was an award accepted, not by the Provincial Workmen's Association Mr. MADDIN,
but in the very words of the deputy minister, by the employees of the company, and it was only by a majority of the employees, for there were a number of lodges of the Provincial Workmen's Association, whose representatives refused to sign the award or accept it. But one would think that when this gentleman came down to the county of Cape Breton to investigate the conditions that obtained there he might possibly have called on the representative of the riding. The hon. minister to-night recommended to the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes) that he should go down to Springhill and tell the men there what Mr. Butler had told him; in other words, he recommends the member for Cumberland to go down to Springhill and tell the men exactly what Mr. Wanklyn toTd the newspaper reporters in June, 1909:	We are going to fight them to a
finish, give us the militia. He recommends the hon. member to go to his constituency and inform those of his constituents who are on strike what Mr. Butler says. If that is his wisdom in this matter, if that is his judgment, if he thinks such action is incumbent on the representative of a constituency where a strike exists, I would think that his deputy, coming to Cape Breton, would have wired me as member for the constituency where the strike existed, and in addition to that the recognized solicitor of the men on strike. I was there in a double capacity, I was the member for the riding and the solicitor of the men.
Does the hon. member mean to say that the deputy minister, when he was there, did not see him?
I could not help seeing him.
He told me distinctly that he made a point of seeing the hon. member, and he was instructed to do so.

I am not taking issue with you there, nor are you taking issue with anything I said. I said I would have thought he would have notified me he was coming, either as solicitor for the men on strike or as representative of the county. Now if it had been Mr. O'Donohoe, who furnishes these plastic reports to the Trades and Labour Council, how he would have been notified and embraced on the arrival of the deputy minister. I received no notification. I saw Mr. Acland, in Glace Bay, with Mr. J. K. L. Ross, son of the president of the company, )vho drew $10,000 a year for doing little or nothing. I saw him accompanied by Mr. Dick, the sales agent of the Coal Company; I saw him going around with the nabobs of this concern. I rode from Glace Bay to Reserve Junction sitting across a sideseated

oar from Mr. Acland, and I was told he was the deputy minister. I had never met him, if he were in the House now he would tell you I had never met him before a passenger said: that is the deputy minister, and he was with these nabobs I have mentioned. He got off at Reserve Junction. That was his second day down in the strike district, gathering information for that report to lay before this parlia-. ment and yet up to that time he had not come to see the member for the county nor the solicitor for the men who were on strike. He knew where I was engaged from 8 o'clock in the morning until midnight in Glace Bay, and when I went home on a certain evening at 6 o'clock, I found a card: F. A. Acland, Deputy Minister of Labour. My good dame said to me: Mr. Acland left the card at the house and said he would like to see you before he left town; he is at the Sydney Hotel. And so I saw him and he was anxious to go over to the north riding to consult with the hon. member who represents that riding, where there was no strike. He was going over on the boat in a few minutes and he said to me, just before going to the boat: I would like to have your opinion about this matter. I said: Have you got the opinion of the men who are in charge of the strike? He replied that he had seen two or three of the executive officers, whom he named. I told him that they had authority to speak about the situation and could doubtless have told him all I could tell him. He asked me about the conditions of order there. I gave him my opinion about the militia. He has not incorporated it in his report. There was not a word in it that should not have been printed, although I felt like saying a good many that would not look well in print. This emissary of the Department of Labour who had journeyed down so far and who on the day on which he was leaving town left a card at my house in Sydney with a pretty positive knowledge that I was in Glace Bay, and would not get out until the evening, and whose anxiety to consult with the hon. gentleman, the member for Cape Breton North (Mr. McKenzie).

May I interrupt my hon. friend. Knowing Mr. Acland as I do, I feel that any action of that kind is not of a sort of which he is capable. I know Mr. Acland to be honourable in the highest degree, and that in going on a mission of this kind he would do his utmost to see every party concerned. I am sorry he is not here at the present moment, but I will have no hesitation in saying that I am quite sure if he did not see my hon. friend the moment he arrived, it was not because of any direct intention not to do so, but that he had every desire to see every person he should see. The hon. member says
that Mr. Acland saw the representatives of the men, and I presume he thought it better to see the men themselves before he saw their solicitor.

I have every regard for the hon. gentleman who acts as deputy for the Minister of Labour. I have not imputed nor do I impute to him anything disloyal to the minister. He was serving his master, he was under instructions. I submit that when this department sends a representative into a county, if it be the fortune of that constituency to be represented by a Conservative that is no reason why that Conservative or that representative of the people there should not be communicated with. Take other instances. In this House and during this session I had occasion to refer to the visit of the Board of Railway Commissioners to the county of Cape Breton. They acted in the same way and what was the report from the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte). Why he said it was through the courtesy of the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) who accompanied the board that we were going to have some necessary repairs done to the Terminal wharf in Sydney. I did not know, and was not told that the board were coming to the town or to the county of Cape Breton, but I was told that they were actually going to repair the terminal wharf in Sydney. I suppose, Mr. Chairman, that if the Deputy Minister of Labour's efforts in Cape Breton had been of a conciliatory rather than an aggressive character, if he had succeeded in stopping the strike we would have been told that it was through the efforts of the hon. member for North Cape Breton, whom he went to see that very evening, that the strike had been amicably adjusted. I have no reference to being slighted personally. I have no desire to get in the private cars of the Board of Railway Commissioners or to ride around with them at all but I would like to know when they are coming to South Cape Breton, and I would like to extend them a little hospitality, and take them around the confines of the city. I would like to do as much for the Deputy Minister of Labour, or the Minister of Labour, when they come there in their official capacity, but, if they come like a thief in the night, if, I am only to see the Deputy Minister of Labour on a street car twelve miles away from the Intercolonial railway station at which he had landed, and then have him pointed out to me by strangers, I submit it is not doing justice to the man who is elected by the common people as their representative nor is it treating the solicitor of the United Mine Workers of America with the slightest measure of consideration. I hold the Department of Labour responsible for this, and not the

deputy. Common courtesy would have imposed on the minister himself, when he sent his deputy down there, the necessity of giving the instruction : Notify Mr. Mad-din that you are going down ; wire him, or, he could have wired me himself and we might have been able to discuss the situation. But no, this gentleman comes down, prepares a report and summarizes the situation on pages 11 and 12. He says :
Many people who are entirely opposed to the United Mine Workers of America and wholly friendly to the Grand Secretary of the Provincial Workmen's Association, state that that official's extended retention of office was a source of discontent among a number of miners. He had become well known to the officials of a number of companies, including the Dominion Coal Company, and had grown into the habit of dealing with the companies on behalf of the men without always going through the form of consulting the men's committees. In this and other ways he had aroused the suspicion and jealousies of a number.
And, now, Mr. Chairman, listen to this gem that we have from the student who went down to study the conditions. He says :
In addition, politics came in. Moffat is frankly a Liberal

I would like the minister to inquire from his deputy where his deputy found out that Moffat was frankly a Liberal. He says :
Moffat is frankly a Liberal, but claims not to have taken unfair advantage of this fact in his capacity as Grand Secretary. He was opposed for Grand Secretary some years ago by Mr. James Madden, now counsel for the United Mine Workers of America, and Conservative member of parliament for the riding.
There is wisdom for. you from the man who left his card at my house, and said that he would like to see me, the man who met me and who did see me but who did not ask me one word about it. In 1901, eight years before the strike, when a very callow youth, I did contest with Mr. Moffat for the position of Grand Secretary of the Provincial Workmen's Association. In 1906 when I ran for the local legislature in Nova Scotia, Moffat took the hustings and campaigned against me. I had the first Conservative majority within the town of Dominion, where he lived for ten years, and in which he took the hustings against me, that had taken place since the town was incorporated. But, in 1904, where was Mr. Moffat, this man who was frankly a Liberal f-supporting Stephen B. McNeil the Labour candidate, a man who could not find anything rank or vile enough to say against Alexander Johnston when he was contesting the county in the interest of the Liberal party and who won. Not content with going through the district, at the Lyceum, the theatres and the rinks', Mr. MADDIN.
he journeyed into the country districts, went amongst the farmers and fishermen, and gave them his opinion of Mr. Johnston and the Grit and Tory governments. That was in 1904. In 1906 he shot his bolt in favour of Kendall and Gillies, and in 1908 there was not a man in the Dominion of Canada in a position to say that he did not vote for me. I have no reason to believe but what he did vote for me. I may say that there is no political difference between us, he certainly did not take the hustings against me, he certainly had no grudge against me, and he certainly made? no canvass against me. On the contrary, I am assured by some of his brother grand officers of the Provincial Workmen's Association that I had his assistance and support in the campaign of 1908, and yet the deputy minister says that :
He was opposed for Grand Secretary some years ago by Mr. James Madden.
Whoever that may be. He doubtless thought it was I. He did not know my name or how to spell it, but he says that ' Mr. Madden ' ran against Moffat, ' who is frankly a Liberal.' I would like to find out where the deputy minister got that information. The whole thing summed up is that there was politics in the situation. True, the Sydney ' Record,' the Glace Bay ' Gazette,' and Mr. Pearson's papers in Halifax and Glace Bay said so, but, when they alleged that the strike arose out of politics, that it was promulgated and promoted for the purpose of making political capital they were uttering falsehoods, which were not only false but false with the knowledge of those who penned and published them. Political capital is ballots marked in favour of the party who seeks the political capital, and I want to review the political occurrences of the province of Nova Scotia, and show him that these base slanders are absolutely unfounded. In 1906 I had the honour of being a candidate for the local legislature in the province of Nova Scotia. I was running with Mr. Butts of North Sydney against Dr. Arthur Kendall and Neil J. Gillies of Glace Bay. Mr. Gillies was an underground manager at one time. He was a past Grand Master Workman of the Provincial Workmens' Association, and he was the candidate of the mining districts.
The hon. member for North Cape Breton had been elected for that constituency in the general election of 1901, he had a plurality of over 2,000 votes. Mr. Butts and I ran the election under those circumstances, and when the ballots were counted on the night of the 20th of June it was midnight before they knew whether Mr. Gillis or I had been elected, and on a recount of the ballots it was found that the Liberal majority of 2,000 plus which the hon. member for North Cape Breton had in 1901 had

dwindled down to 120. Where did these votes come from-a majority of over 275 from the town of Sydney Mines in the riding of North Cape Breton, and I led tire poll in Mr. Gillis' home throughout the southern mining districts. The miners in 1906 in Cape Breton county voted for Butts and Maddin. In the county of Pictou Mr. Tanner had a plurality of 454 in the town of Westville a small mining town and in the Back Mines district in the town of Stellarton, and away from the round house and the influence of the Intercolonial railway Mr. Tanner also had a majority. The complete returns from the province of Nova Scotia in the local election of 1906 showed that the Conservative candidates had a majority amongst the miners of Cumberland county of over 500, that the Conservative candidates in Pictou county had a majority among the miners of over 500, and that Mr. Butts and I had a majority in the county of Cape Breton of over 500. There was political capital among the miners of the province. In 1908 how was it? The hon. member for Cumberland took a majority of 500 out of the county of Cumberland, and a majority of 300 in the town of Springhill alone. Mr. Tanner who opposed the member for Pictou had a majority of over 500 in the county pf Pictou and in the county of North Cape Breton Mr. McCormack had a majority of over 200 in the town of Sydney Mines among the miners there. I stand 'here to-night as the representative of the votes of the miners of Cape Breton who gave me in the south riding a majority of between 400 and 500 in the mining districts. There was political capital again in 1908. And, you can run the whole gamut of the Grit newspapers in the province of Nova Scotia from the ' Morning Chronicle ' down to the Glace Bay ' Gazette ' or from ' Free Speech ' or the ' Vindicator ' down to the Sydney ' Record ' and they are all filled with the idea that the matter is promoted for political purposes. Why, Sir, the interest of the Liberal Conservative party in the province of Nova Scotia lies in continued work, double shift, opening up new collieries, steady employment, that would have meant more political capital to the Conservative party than a strike with its incidental horrors. The emigration which takes place, the people who leave the country whether the strike lasts for a week or a month going from the mining districts operates to the disadvantage of the Liberal Conservative party. And the Liberal Conservative party as a party was the only party who had anything to loose, and the Liberal party is the only party which had anything to gain by keeping the strike going and that may account for the diffidence and backwardness of the department in dealing with the situation of South Cape
Breton and Springhill. I have taken up more time than I intended when I commenced to speak and there are some publications that I would like to have before the committee and which I probably will present for their consideration at a future day.

I have listened very attentively to the observations of the hon. member for South Cape Breton. He has wandered over a very wide field, and has spoken about a great many things which I do not think on reflection he will consider have very much bearing on the question before the chair. I do not know that this House is very much concerned about the number of votes that were cast at Glace Bay in the local elections of 1906 or the number of votes that were cast at Sydney Mines, or the number of votes that may have been cast at some municipal election in different parts of Nova Scotia. If my hon. friend wants to make a general statement about the political complexion of the province of Nova Scotia he could sum it up in a very short statement; he can say that since confederation the province of Nova Scotia has been in the hands of the Liberal party continuously with the exception of one lean four years that it happened to be in the hands of the Tories. The people of the province had a taste of what they were capable of doing for one four years, and they pitched them out of office at the very earliest opportunity and ever since 1882 they never had a look in, to use a vulgar expression, in the government of Nova Scotia.
I would like to ask my hon. friend what his observations, from the time he rose until the present moment have to do with the motivin'
My hon. friend has given such little attention to the business of this House this winter he possibly doesn't know anything that is going on.

I wish to repudiate that on the spot. I paid as much attention to the business of this House as the hon. member, and the chances are, with a great deal more advantage to the country, and this is the time and place to say so.

My hon. friend may have had messengers back and forth to this House telling him what was going on, but I will venture to say that he graced this House very little during the session with his presence.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to make myself clear
Order.

You will get all the order you want. I would like to make myself

clear with regard to this matter. I would like to know what the hon. member means by ' presence ' in the House. I wonder if he conveys an imputation behind it; I wonder if he would like a Roland for his Oliver?

I do not know what my, hon. friend means by a Roland for his Oliver. If he says that he is Dr. Jeckel and Mr. Hyde and that Mr. Hyde was here and Dr. Jeckel was absent or that he is some double personage I don't know anything about it; all I know is that the honourable Mr. Maddin whom I regard as the representative for South Cape Breton has been absent in the body the most of the *session, and that he was not here is what I mean by saying that he was not present. That is about as plain as I can say it, and I think my hon. friend will understand it. He may have been better engaged, I am not making any insinuation.
Mr. Chairman-
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Unless the hon. gentleman who has the floor permits, another hon. member may not interrupt.
I will ask for his leave.
There are some explanations due to his constituents from the hon. member why he was not here, and he can make them.

That is very good indeed, and I appreciate the courtesy and the big heartedness and the benevolent and the generosity of the hon. member for Cape Breton. If he wishes to put me in competition with himself or some other hon. members as to the number of hours I spend behind a desk in this chamber, I think he has perhaps sat longer behind his desk than I have. But there is this to say, that at any time that I was absent from my chair I was within the precincts of the House, and when I have been there I have contributed more to the development, improvement and welfare of this country in one hour than the hon. member usually does in ten hours, and have given less offence in doing so.
_ Mr. McKENZIE. I thought that according to the hon. member for South Cape Breton, it was left to the hon. Minister of Labour to give glowing pictures of himself; but it seems that there are other picture painters in this country, and they are of the class I heard described by the Minister of Agriculture once this session, as painters who paint things not, as they are, but as they would like them to be. That is about the description which the hon. member for South Cape Breton is giving of himself; but it is certainly not the picture of the hon. member which this Mr. MADDIN.
House knows. Now, the general complexion of politics in Nova Scotia can be put in very small compass. After iorty years of continuous Liberal rule, there is not one county in the province of Nova Scotia today represented altogether by Conservatives. Out of thirty-eight members in the provincial legislature there are I think five members representing the principles of the party of which my hon. friend boasts. That is all he has to encourage him in the conditions of local politics in the province. I do not think it was necessary for my hon. friend to introduce politics into this matter at all. He is not going to drag me into casting any reflection, one way or the other, on the men who were concerned in the strike in Cape Breton. My hon. friend would give you to understand that that strike was something like strikes in other parts of the province. As a rule, when men are out on strike, they are all out. It is a question of the men on one side and the corporation or employers on the other side. Such was not the case in the county of Cape Breton. It was simply a division among the men themselves, about one-half on one side and one-half on the other side; Provincial Workmen's Association men on one side, satisfied with the conditions under which they laboured with the company, stayed with the company; and on the other side the followers and supporters of the United Mine Workers. That was the situation. My hon. friend from South Cape Breton at once destroyed his usefulness to the people he represented by allying himself with one camp of the mep. It was his duty and his responsibility, as the representative of that county, as the representative of the Provincial Workmen's Association men just as much as the United Mine Workers men, to conserve his duty to them all by keeping clear and not becoming the lawyer or adviser of on.e party more than the other. The moment my hon. friend became the lawyer and adviser and strategist of the United Mine Workers men, that moment he lost the confidence of at least one-half the workingmen of his county, and made it absolutely impossible for the Department of Labour to consult him as to what should be done. I say that advisedly, because the moment the Department of Labour consulted Mr. Maddin, one-half the men would say, to the deputy minister: Of what use is it for you to come here as representing the Department of Labour and expect to do fairly by us when you consult the lawyer on the other side? Therefore it was advisable for the Deputy Minister of Labour to get his information elsewhere than from the solicitor of one camp which was engaged in a pitched battle at the time with the other. The hon. member says that I was consulted in the matter by the Deputy Minister of Labour.

I did not make such a
statement. I said that the Deputy Minister of Labour, when he called on me, said that he wanted to go across the harbour to consult with Mr. McKenzie. I did not say that he did consult with the hon member or that Mr. McKenzie advised him.

As men of affairs and men of some common sense, I think we are bound to draw the inference from the statement of the hon. member in regard to the deputy minister being in such a hurry that he would not talk to him, but wanted to go across the harbour and talk to the member for North Cape Breton, that the deputy minister was going to consult me about the matter in hand. In justice to the deputy minister, I must say that he never discussed with me anything connected with the trouble in the southern part of the county. There were troubles brewing in my own part of the county at that time. There was some rumbling that the men at Sydney Mines were coming out. Fortunately they did not. But they were negotiating for a conciliation board, and I spoke to the deputy minister about that. I felt that I had enough to do in trying to keep things quite in my own district without interfering with the southern district, and I did not interfere at all. The point I thought my hon. friend was going to make was in connection with the Industrial Disputes Act. He is a lawyer of some experience and capacity, and he has been dealing with that Act since 1907. He has had exceptional opportunity in this House of dealing with any weaknesses which he might find in that Act; but I have not heard of him making any suggestion as to how it could be made better or more workable than it is. I was thinking, before the hon. gentleman sat down, that he would give us some practical suggestions as to how this Act could be improved.
If there is anything the matter with this Act, why let us sit down and reason together and make it better. I am sure there is not a man here who would not be glad to do so; but at the same time, I must say representing as I do, a great many working men and some capital, that while I want to be fair to the labouring men, I must also, as a member of parliament, be fair to capital. Let us try and constitute a court which will deal fairly with both sides. I cannot understand that it is to the benefit of labouring men in this country that they should be advised or permitted to take an unfair advantage of their employers. I do not think that is what they want. What they want is a fair ' deal; and if this Act can be improved upon so that a better condition of things may be brought about and a fairer trial given,
I am sure no one will be more pleased than myself, but why should my hon.
friend spend hours threshing in this House the old straw, about the different things that happened when that unfortunate conflict was on at Glace Bay. I am sure he must admit that the strike was ill advised and badly conducted and resulted in disaster and defeat to the men. It has brought forth no good; and if the men had any grievances, I am sorry they did not meet with more success in having these grievances remedied. Knowing the labouring men as I do, I can say that there is not in Nova Scotia or anywhere east of Winnipeg, a class of people better paid, better housed or more comfortable than the miners of the county of Cape Breton. They are intelligent people, wishing to give a fair return to their employers and capable of understanding fair treatment if they are well advised. I think it is admitted by nine-tenths of the men who went on this strike, that they were ill advised and the hon. gentleman, who boasts so loudly of being their legal adviser, has nothing to brag about as regards the way in which the strike was conducted and concluded. These men were left at last to the mercy of the Dominion Coal Company without any protection whatever; they were left to shift for themselves without reaching any conclusion that will be beneficial to them.
I shall not say anything further about the political effect. We had an election down there a few days ago, and I shall allow my hon. friend to count the votes and let him tell the House what happened there last Thursday.
An effort has been made to show undue haste in bringing out the militia. The difficulty is, that when men introduce politics into everything, it is impossible for them to be fair. Does the hon. gentleman forget that the Militia Act has been on our statutes for over 30 years just as it stands to-day ? Does he forget that it is the product and creation of his own party friends, and that the clauses providing for calling out the military to help the civil powers are to-day just as they were from the beginning ? All that is necessary is to make certain affidavits and comply with certain provisions and no Minister of Militia can refuse military aid. My hon, friend tries to make political capital among men who do not understand these things by saying that the Minister of Militia had no business to send out the troops; but he will not dare say that Mr. Justice Finlayson would think of granting an order calling for the troops, unless the necessity for so doing was clearly established. The Mayor of Glace Bay was appealed to for further assistance in the way of furnishing policemen to keep the trouble down and what did he do ? What was the sage advice he gave ? I will give you aid, he said, 500 strikers to act as policemen. Did you ever

hear of such an absuidity ?	500 of those
who were on strike and against whom the property of the company had to be protected, the mayor suggested, should act as its guardians.	,
Another point my hon. friend tried to make, was that the county of Cape Breton was taxed for the payment of these men. I presume, as far as the municipalities are concerned, that we all have to pay our share. That is the law. If any municipality calls for the aid of the troops, it has to pay the extra expense, and that would have been the case in the county of Inverness, or Pictou, ot Guysborough, had the demand been made in any of these. Why were not the volunteer militia called out, my hon. friend asked._ He thinks there would have been a saving of money if they had been, but he knows very well, that he is not putting the whole truth before the House in that connection. The only charge against the town of Glace Bay or the county of Cape Breton is the_ difference between the cost of the militia from the barracks at Halifax and their cost when in active service on the field. When officers are engaged in the field they are paid higher wages than when in the barracks and I presume so also are the soldiers; and whatever may be the difference, it has to be paid by the municipality. I presume the county of Cape Breton had to pay the expense of transportation, but the same amount of money which would be paid these men in barracks is paid by the government and not one cent of that is paid by the county.
Hon. gentlemen opposite applauded the case made out by my hon. friend, but if they heard the case as it is being tried out in "the courts, there would be no * hear, hears,' from any hon. member on either side who understands the situation and the Militia Act. An effort however, is being made, to poison the minds of the people, particularly interested by giving them a false side of the showing. I do not think it is necessary to discuss this matter at any length. The only thing open to my hon. friend to show is in what way this Act could be improved. If he has any proposal to that effect, I am sure it will receive fair consideration at the hands of the government and this House, but so far, he has given us none, and therefore, he might well have spared us the meandering statements he has been making to no purpose.
He attacked the courts that have been constituted for the purpose of inquiries of this kind in the province of Nova Scotia, but when asked for particulars he had to admit that he had no fault to find with any one of them? What objection could he have to men like Prof. Shortt, or Mr. Justice Graham, of the Supreme Court of Mr. McKenzie
Nova Scotia, or Mr. Justice Paterson, or Mr. Justice MacGilvray, who have sat from time to time upon those courts? Why, my hon. friend himself has been a member of a conciliation court. He forgot to tell us that. And what was the result of his great wisdom as a member of that court? He was dealing with one of the mines of the Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company, and he signed, as the third arbitrator, a report which was signed by all, reducing the wages of the men.. He had not the slightest objection to the powers he was given as arbitrator, nor to any of the proceedings. And he came before the miners of Sydney Mines and read them a lecture, declaring that they should accept this result and be satisfied that the Act was giving them everything that was coming to them.
Was his decision just and proper?

I am not saying whether it was or not. But it was a decision reached under the operation of this Act. And if a just decision could be reached in that investigation by Mr. Mad-din and two other men, Prof. Shortt being one, what particular charm had Mr. Mad-din in connection with that inquiry that was not present at the other inquiry?
Why did not the Minister of Labour do as Mr. Maddin did and bring about a correct decision?
Does my hon. friend (Mr. Lancaster), who professes to be a-lawyer-
I am not professing to be anything; I am trying to understand from the hon. gentleman what he is driving at. Will he permit me to ask him a question?
I will answer his first question, and then he can ask me another. He asks: Why did not the minister see to it that the decision of the board was a correct one?
Why did he object-

I will give the answer. Does the hon. gentleman sav that, if a decision of the Supreme Court is reversed bv the Privy Council the government should be called to task and told that they should see to it that the court shall give only such decisions as will be sustained? That is the position he takes when he asks why the Minister of Labour does not see to it that every decision given by a conciliation board shall be such as will be sustained by the men.

The hon. gentleman, inadvertently, of course, has misunderstood what I said. I asked why it was not

competent for the minister to bring about a lust decision which he says Mr. Maddin brought about when he was a member of
a board?
Mi\ McKENZIE. Perhaps I am one of tnosc unfortunate Scotchmen upon whom a surgical operation must be performed in order to make him understand, but I must admit that I cannot understand the question of my hon. friend. There is an Act of this parliament which enables a court to be constituted under certain conditions, and he charges the minister who puts that law in operation with the duty of seeing to it that every court so constituted shall reach a decision of a certain character.
I say an equitable and just decision.

What is equitable and just depends upon the viewpoint. What I might regard as equitable and just might be regarded as quite the contrary by somebody else. It depends upon whose ox is gored, as the old saying is. It is absolutely absurd to say that the power that appoints a judge or creates a court can be held responsible for the decisions that court may reach.
The hon. gentleman .was a judge himself at one time, was he not?

Yes. I was, and I should have thought it very absurd, indeed, if the powers that appointed me had been held responsible for any eccentricity that might be found in my decisions. I think it would be as profitable for my hon. friend to leave me alone and let me finish the few observations I have to make.
Certainly.

An effort was made by my hon. friend from South Cape Breton (Mr. Maddin) to cast unfavourable reflections upon the member for Cape Breton m the local house (Dr. Kendall). I am sure Dr. Kendall does not require defence at my hands, so far as his efforts in support of the labouring classes are concerned, and I am not going to say anything further about it. But from what I can gather from the observations of the hon. member, they were entirely aimed at making political capital, and did not suggest anything that would better the conditions of the working men either in Cape Breton or in any other part of the province. I am sure that anything I say in answer to him must not be undei stood as opposed to doing everything possible for the working men of my county.
At the same time, I think it would be advisable for myself and my hon. friend (Mr. Maddin) to keep clear of being counsel for one body of our constituents as against a body on the other side if we hope to con-109
serve our usefulness in bringing them together. I commend the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes) for having kept himself free from entanglements that would destroy his usefulness as a promoter of good understanding among these classes. Had the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Maddin) done the same he might have assisted the Department bf Labour in improving existing relations. I am sorry he felt it necessary to make such reflections upon the Minister of Labour; I am sorry to find a disposition on the part of hon. members of the opposition in this House to make attacks upon that hon. gentleman. If he were no good, if he were r.ot a credit to the party to which he belongs, to the government of which he is a member, and to the cause he represents, they would have patted him on the back and told him he was all right. It is an old saying that it is under the good apple-tree that you find sticks and stones. I think the Minister of Labour (Mr. King) can take it as a compliment that these attacks are being made upon him. I hope he will not take the observations of the hon. member for South Cape Breton in any way serious. They do not mean anything-he does not mean anything by them himself.
I can assure the hon. minister that the people of eastern Nova Scotia who have to deal with great industrial matters will have the same confidence in him, and, indeed, a great deal more, than if he were applauded by the hon. member for South Cape Breton. As I have said. I stand here as a representative of labour, ready and willing to bring about any betterments that may be made by the Court of Inquiry constituted to investigate any difficulties that may arise between capital and labour in any part of the Dominion of Canada, particularly the part that I myself represent.

After a speech of half an hour by the hon. gentleman from North Cape Breton in which he said a lot about inferences he was compelled to draw, I do not know whether or not he is in favour of voting this money.
I am in favour of the vote.

My hon. friend should have deferred arriving at that conclusion until a little later. Of course, in his speech there was not a word about party politics, no suggestion whatever on politics from this legal luminary who descended from the calm precincts of the bench to take part in party warfare. Turning the spear which he levelled against me back upon himself,
I would ask him to search his own conscience a little and see to what extent his nice little compliment to the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes) that his speech was so commendable and free from

any party questions would apply to his own remarks. This hon. gentleman who goes upon the bench, who tries cases there and then leaves the bench after about two years' occupancy to go into the party strife of politics, into the most vigorous contests, 1 who escapes defeat by very small majorities and persistent running in all that party strife, who takes the time of this House for nearly half an hour on an item in regard to $27,300 without even stating whether he is in favour of the item being voted or not, has no justification for criticising as he did the address of the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Mad-din) who has made a very strong and important statement in regard to matters that did pertain to the item before the Chair. When the hon. member disparages the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Maddin) he forgets his own history, that he descended from the bench to take part in this very party warfare, and I think that we must not be blamed in the future if we pay no attention whatever to anything that falls from his lips in regard to this or any other matter.
The hon. member has said that the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Maddin) has made no suggestions, has shown nothing wrong with this Act. The hon. member for North Cape. Breton (Mr. McKenzie) may have been writing or reading letters in his seat, for he does very little else in the way of useful legislation in this House, or he would have heard as the rest of us did, the most pertinent suggestions as to the defects in this Act. As was prophesied by several of us, including the leader of the opposition, when this Act was being passed, it has turned out in a disastrous way. This Act is unfair and never can be made fair as it is drawn. The right of the men to strike is suspended until it is of no earthly use to them. As I illustrated two years 'ago when this was brought in it is like saying to the men : We will not prevent you from eating fruit, but you must wait until the fruit is rotten before you do so. It is the same sort of pretended benefit which is nothing but a gold brick. The man is not permitted to strike until the strike will do him no good or until there is nothing left to strike about or until he is starved to death, or must leave the country in order to avoid being starved. The Act is not working fairly to the workingman. If the Minister of Labour is not going to take any more interest in it than he has up to this time the only right thing to do is to repeal that Act and not have it on the statutejbook, where it is an invitation to people to believe that they have legislation that is some good to them but which is really nothing but a broken reed that gives way under them when they try to lean on it. The Minister of Labour must Mr. LANCASTER.
not trifle with this any longer ; he must make the Act workable so that the men will have some chance to get a reasonable arbitrament under it in time to do some good or else repeal the Act, and not pretend he is defending or protecting or getting justice for the labouring man. As we prophesied when the Act was drawn, the men are induced to believe that the government are acting as a guardian over wards, to see that they get fair play, and need not resort to strikes, to get these rights and remedies and yet nothing was to be done for them because the pull of the capitalist was of more importance to the government than the cries or screams or murmurings of the labouring man and his family. The Minister of Labour seems to-night to be perfectly willing to have a hypocritical piece of legislation on the statute-book which is of no use to the working man, and it would be better, safer, more honest to the workman to repeal the Act and say : You must look out for yourself as before, we are no guardians of yours. When a deputy minister is sent down to inquire into the merits of the case he seems to think that when he has pointed out that one man is a Conservative and the other a Liberal that is all that is required to form a decision. I do not think it is fair that the Minister of Labour should take the position he does in this matter, and I as a member of this House protest against this money being voted for any such purpose as the Minister of Labour appears to be using it for.

In his remarks on this subject this evening the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie), in referring to a possible excuse for the Deputy Minister of Labour not calling upon me when he came down to Cape Breton in 1901, stated that he should not have come to me, I being the solicitor for the men on strike, and therefore, that I was taking sides. I am very glad that it has remained for the. hon. member for Cape Breton to say that; I am very glad indeed that the gentleman who occupies the portfolio of Minister of Labour did not offer that as an excuse. He got up to defend his depuity and he said that he regretted this lack of courtesy, and that it was not intentional. What does the hon. member for North Cape Breton say with regard to a situation such as this? He says that the deputy minister should not have called on me, because, forsooth, I was the solicitor of one of the sides to the strike. Has he so little wit, has he so little judgment as to imagine that one union was fighting the other? The men on strike were fighting the com-* pany.

I certainly did not ; say so. I said that two bodies of men

were fighting each other, the United Mine Workers' and the Provincial Workmens' Association, that the hon. gentleman was the solicitor of one side of the men, not as against the company at ail.
The deputy minister did not see the hon. gentleman until he was through with both sides of the men and their officers. Then he saw the hon. gentleman.

When he came to my house with his card, is the hon. gentleman going to impute that he was playing the hypocrite? Does he know that he had seen both sides before he left that card at my house? Did he call knowing that I was away, and that he would not see me?
I would like the hon. gentleman who is a lawyer, and an ex-judge to exercise the function of ordinary every day common sense which, as a jurist and a lawyer, and a member of this House, he has not always exercised, I would ask him to exercise it to-night and to explain it to the committee how the deputy minister left his card at my house during the day with the request to meet him unless he was pre-109J
pared to meet me when he came to my house. Was -he playing the hypocrite knowing that I was not there when he came with his card pretending that he .was friendly to me and willing to interview me? The hon. member for North Cape Breton places himself on the horns of a very awkward dilemma. On the one hand it is little credit to the hon. gentleman, and on the other it is little credit to the deputy minister. There is one observation that I wish to make. The hon. member for North Cape Breton stepped aside tonight to cast an aspersion on my personal integrity as a member of a board of conciliation, and spoke of how I had found against the miners down in Cape Breton at one time and had gone to a building and talked them into submission. He thought it an extraordinary thing that the member for South Cage Breton should recommend and approve a reduction of wages. The hon. member for North Cape Breton occupied the very seat on the county comt bench that is now occupied by the gentleman to whom I paid tribute to-night, and he did not always discharge his duties there with the dignity, fairness and uprightness that have characterized his successor, but rather with the attitude, and in the manner in which he has discussed this matter which is before the committee to-night. He referred to my acting on the board of conciliation, and he said that I had gone to the miners of Cape Breton and tried to persuade them to accept a reduction of wages. Earlier in the evening, while discussing this matter with the Minister of Labour, I pointed out to him that when the books of the company were exhibited to a member of the board it was not for the purpose of the public, but only for the information of the members of the board. Let me read to you from section 13 of the Act, the oath which a member of the board takes, and the oath which I as a member of that board, to which the hon. member refers, did take. It is this:
13. Before entering upon the exercise of the functions of their office the members of a board, including the chairman, shall make oath or affirmation before a justice of the peace that they will faithfully and impartially perform the duties of their office, and also that, except in the discharge of their duties, they will not disclose to any person any of the evidence or other matter brought before the board.
I made that oath, I accepted it with the responsibility that I would accept the oath of a judge in the Supreme Court or the county _ court or the oath of a wit-; ness giving evidence before any trii bunal. Acting under that oath, when the books of the company made it apparent to me as a representative of the men

that tor various reasons the increase in the wages of common labourers employed by the Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company at that time could not, from the revenues of the company, be legitimately, honestly, fairly and equitably increased, I joined in a recommendation that a reduction should take place amongst another class of employees of the company. Who were they? Machine runners and shot firers at No. 3 Sydney Mine. Some of those machine runners, according to public and published evidence taken there earned as high as $14 per day-only a very limited number-but there was quite a number who made $7 and $8 per day. With a sense of fairness and equity,- which the men themselves appreciated when I had explained it to them, I thought that they might very well stand a small reduction in order that the common labourers receiving $1.35 might receive $1.43. I went out and submitted that to the men, and I put it up to them as I put up the policy gospel of the Tory party to them, and they accepted the one as they accepted the other. I ask the Minister of Labour if he considers Dr. Adam Shortt, the chairman of the Civil Service Commission an honest and an honourable and an upright man? What does the minister say to that?
I hardly think it is necessary to answer a question of that sort.
Would the minister place any reliance on his opinion of a fellow-member of the board?
I believe the hon. member (Mr. Maddin) would be actuated by the highest sense of honour.

That is not answering my question. I am absolutely indifferent to the opinion of the minister with regard to myself; what I ask him is, does he consider Dr. Adam Shortt, who has served.on nearly 30 boards of conciliation, who occupied the Sir John Macdonald chair in Queens University, who is the foremost economist of the Dominion of Canada, who is- recognized from Vancouver to Sydney as one of the most upright men in Canada; would the minister consider Dr. Shortt's opinion of a colleague on the board of conciliation as being sound and and worthy. Yes or no?
Go on.
I have the very highest opinion of Professor Shortt.
The hon. member (Mr. Carvell) might give his opinion when he is asked.

If you want it I have to say very plainly that you have a lot of
impudence to hold up a member
Order.
I want the opinion in parliamentary language if the hon. member for 'Carleton can put it in parliamentary language.
I can tell my hon. friend that if any member

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am not sure that the hon. gentleman has a right to speak.
He is asking me a question.
I rise to a point of order. I ask that the hon. member (Mr. Carvell) be required to withdraw.
That is all right. The hon. member for Cape Breton and myself cannot have any quarrel; he wants my opinion.

If we are to have matters conducted properly we had better have this ended. I ask that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Carvell) frankly withdraw the statement he made. It is not a matter personal to the members concerned, it is a reflection on the whole House.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: 1 have considered the matter concluded. I understood the hon. member to withdraw.
If the hon. member for Carleton cares to answer the question I propounded to the Minister of Labour, I give him the opportunity of answering it if he can do it in parliamentary language.

I will try to answer in parliamentary language. I tell him that so far as I am concerned I think no member of this House has any right to address a question to the Minister of Labour and demand an answer in the way this question was put, and if I were the Minister of Labour I would not give an answer.

Very well, you have not answered my question. In the report of Dr. Shortt to the Department of Labour on this occasion, he states that he found cases where men made from $3 to $6 and $7, and even $10 and $11 per day, and in one or two instances as much as $13 or $14 per day had been made. I concurred in a recommendation that a reduction be made from the wages of such men and applied to the wages of those who were receiving a smaller sum. To-night I am charged by the hon. member for North Cape Breton that when I was on a board I recommended a reduction, and that I went out to a building to the men to urge them to accept it. Now. Dr. Shortt in his report to the government has this to say, and it is only in self-defence and in justice

to myself that I venture to read the following from Dr. Shortt's report:
My colleague 911 the board, Mr. J. VY. Madam, as the nominee of the miners, had a particularly difficult position to fill, where the award of the board was so little attractive to some of the most influential of the miners. He not only maintained an independent and judicial attitude in arriving at the award of v-v. board, but accepted the fullest responsibility for the award and laboured most actively to secure its adoption.
That is a testimonial that I value as highly as the parchment I received with my degree from Dalhousie College ia 1100. -Now, Mr. Chairman, with this testimonial from Dr. Shortt in these circumstances, my integrity is to be impugned, and by whom? By an hon. member, who, after he had accepted the nomination to run for this House, filed a judgment in his court which was afterwards set aside by the' Supreme Court of Nova Scotia, by a gentler man whom the returns indicate, had no fewer than 125 men appointed as fish wardens in the county of Victoria, and to many streams where no one ever saw water flow during the months they drew the salary for guarding these streams- Little Mountain torrents, Black Brook and such places in the county of Victoria. That is the hon. gentleman who casts aspersion on my integrity, and my honour, and my character, when J was charged with the first and only judicial matter I had the honour to decide. This is my accuser. Why, Sir, I wish to say to you that with the oath I had taken under the provisions of this Industrial Disputes Act, with the knowledge that the men whom I represented had confidence in me, and with the endorsation which will live there in the lecords of this House, from such a man as Dr. Shortt, I think I may feel safe in laughing at the aspersions emanating from such a source as that.
I think it is only fair myself that I should reply to the personal observations made by the hon. member for South Cape Breton. I did not make any personal aspersion upon him about his position. Far from it; 'Hansard' will show' ."id not. I simply said he "was so satisfied with the working of this Act that he acted under it and gave a decision. I .said, and 1 was telling the truth, that he gave a decision recommending a reduction of wages. He has the very ill grace of making a reference to a decision of mine when I was on the bench. I would like to see or hear of any judge that was ever on the bench who had not some of his decisions reversed. There may bt a few but there are very few of them in this country I take it as coming from a man who has' no conception of the dignity of the profession to which he belongs, that he would descend to such low tactics as to make reference to the decision that a man may have given when he was on the bench which may have been reversed by the Supreme Court. That is the only thing in my history of fifty years in the county of Cape Breton with regard to my private character that he evidently thinks he can put his finger upon. I would like to know if the hon. member for South Cape Breton is prepared to make an open book of his conduct and his character in the county of Cape Breton for the few years he has been there.
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has put a question, and I would like to answer it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman cannot even answer the question unless permission is given.

I am forced to make an answer. The hon. gentleman makes further reference to guardians who were appointed over fisheries. I say the statement is absolutely false, a deliberate lie, with the knowledge of its being a falsehood and a deliberate lie.
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. It is not allowable to attribute deliberate falsehood to any member of this House.
I say the statement is a deliberate falsehood.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Even in that form I think the statement is beyond parliamentary latitude.
Perhaps it is. *

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: In that case I must ask the hon. gentleman to withdraw it.
I will put it in another shape.
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is at liberty to change the statement to a form that is in order.

I rise to order. I submit that when a member of this House calls your attention to the fact that another member has made a statement which is contrary to the usage of this House, before the hon. gentleman can make any further statement, he must withdraw the statement which you have ruled out of order. He must withdraw that statement absolutely before he can say anything more, and that is what I ask you to direct him to do.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think that the decision having been given, the hon. member for South Simcoe is correct. It is the right of the hon. member, before the

decision is given, to explain his words and to place what he has stated in another form which would be within the rules of the House. I think that in this case the decision has been given, and so I would ask the hon. member to withdraw the statement.
I propose, if it is necessary, to deal with this question along the lines suggested by the Chair. If I were outside of this House I would not withdraw the statement.
Order, order.
If it is not parliamentary here, I would withdraw it. As I said, if I were outside of this House I would not withdraw it, I have the right now to put it in another shape.
I rise to a point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. ' The hon. member is, I believe, in the process of withdrawing the statement. The withdrawal is not necessary in a single word. He has announced his purpose to withdraw and has absolutely withdrawn the statement, and he is proceeding now to place it in what he considers it a correct form.
I am not aware of any cause of a point of order in what he has said. If the hon. member believes there is, I will hear his point of order.

As I understand, the hon. gentleman aggravated the original offence by deliberately stating that he withdrew the offensive expression only, in response to the demand of the chair, and that if he were outside _ of the House he would repeat it. It is new doctrine to me, if that is a parliamentary withdrawal of an offensive expression. Now, I think it is due to the dignity of this House that we should have thorough understanding of whether we are governed by parliamentary rule

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. member must adhere strictly to the point of order and not discuss the dignity of the House or any other matter.
Mr Chairman, if necessary, I would like to appeal to the Speaker, because I think this is a very serious matter. I am serious, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. member for Cape Breton wishes to discuss that point of order, Ee is at liberty to do it.

I have already stated that in compliance with' parliamentary procedure I have withdrawn the statement.
I say that the purpose of the hon. member for South Cape Breton was to charge me with dishonesty in my election, by saying that in order to get elected I had made appointments which I had no business to make. I say that he cannot sustain that contention; there is no evidence to support it, and I challenge him either from the records of parliament or anywhere else to sustain it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the point of order is clear. The hon. gentleman has stated that he withdrew the expression that had been objected to. To that he had added the expression that outside of the House he would deal otherwise with it. I think the point of order raised by the hon. member for New Westminster is correct, that it would be an evasion of a withdrawal to state that outside of the House he would do otherwise. But in the statement made by the hon. member for South Cape Breton at the present time of rising, he has clearly withdrawn without adding the objectionable portion, so that I believe he is now within the rules of the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the hon. member for New Westminster is serious in saying that he desires further information on this item, ( would move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again, because it is too late to continue to-night.

Before the committee rises, I would not want the hon. member for North Cape Breton to go away with any misapprehension of my statement, wliich he takes so heavily to heart. I did not say that he had made a decision which was set aside. All our judges do that, because they are human. All of them give hcnest, well-meant judgments which are l set aside. What I did say was, that after

he had accepted a nomination he had delivered a judgment which was afterwards set aside. That is a mere statement of a fact, and I did not mention it because his judgment had been set aside. Any one's judgment is liable to be set aside.
